package main

import (
	"fmt"
	"net/http/httptest"

	"github.com/gin-gonic/gin"
)

func main() {
	gin.SetMode(gin.TestMode)
	r := gin.New()
	trace := []string{}
	r.Use(func(c *gin.Context) { trace = append(trace, "before"); c.Next(); trace = append(trace, "after") })
	v1 := r.Group("/v1")
	v1.GET("/health", func(c *gin.Context) { trace = append(trace, "handler"); c.JSON(200, gin.H{"ok": true}) })
	w := httptest.NewRecorder()
	r.ServeHTTP(w, httptest.NewRequest("GET", "/v1/health", nil))
	fmt.Println(w.Code, trace) // 200 [before handler after]
}

sections.walkthrough: go get records gin v1.12.0 in go.mod and the hashes of Gin and its dependencies in go.sum. go run . builds and starts the package in the current directory. The curl line answers only once main hosts the engine in an http.Server, as shown later in this lesson. Run these commands in your own development environment; the first download needs access to the Go module proxy.

sections.body: Put route registration in a function such as newRouter. It returns a fully configured *gin.Engine and has no side effects: no listening socket, no global state beyond Gin's mode. The example registers a fixed health route and a route with a :name parameter, then sends three requests through ServeHTTP and prints the status and body of each one.
sections.title: Build the engine and register routes
sections.walkthrough: gin.SetMode(gin.TestMode) runs before the engine is built, so Gin does not print its debug route table. ServeHTTP is the same method http.Server would call; httptest.NewRecorder captures the status and body. /health renders JSON, /hello/gopher binds "gopher" to :name, and /missing falls through to Gin's default 404 handler, which writes the plain body "404 page not found".

sections.body: gin.Default() is gin.New() plus the Logger and Recovery middleware. That is convenient for a demo, but a service usually wants to choose its own access log format, fields and destination. Starting from gin.New() makes every piece of the chain visible in one place, which is also where a reviewer will look first when a request misbehaves.
sections.title: gin.Default versus gin.New
sections.walkthrough: This fragment is the explicit form of gin.Default(). Order matters: middleware registered with Use runs for every route added after it, in registration order. requestLogger is a placeholder for the slog-based middleware built later in this course.

sections.body: r.Run(":8080") is a shortcut that calls http.ListenAndServe with no timeouts. A production process should construct an http.Server so that header, read, write and idle budgets are explicit and so that shutdown can drain in-flight requests. The engine stays exactly the same; only its host changes.
sections.title: Serve it with an explicit http.Server
sections.walkthrough: Run this fragment in your own development environment, not inside the app sandbox. ReadHeaderTimeout bounds slow clients that trickle headers; IdleTimeout closes unused keep-alive connections. http.ErrServerClosed is the normal result after Shutdown, so it is not treated as a failure.

sections.body: Because the router is just a Handler, the fastest feedback loop is a table of requests sent through ServeHTTP. That catches a wrong method, a missing slash or a route conflict in milliseconds, with no port allocation and no flaky network. Keep an integration test that starts a real server too, but let the in-process tests carry the bulk of routing and handler behaviour.
sections.title: Test before you listen

readings.takeaway: Return a configured *gin.Engine from a constructor, test it with httptest and ServeHTTP, and host it in an explicit http.Server rather than r.Run when it goes to production.
readings.title: Your first Gin service: an engine, two routes and a test request
wrongAnswers: gin.Default disables networking in test mode

cautions: Trailing-slash redirects are written before middleware, so access logs miss them.
Enabling UseRawPath lets parameters contain '/', which handlers must validate.
designGuide.cost: No runtime cost beyond the radix-tree lookup; the work is deciding a slash and encoding policy and pinning it with a table test.
strengths: Conflicting templates fail at registration, before any traffic.
FullPath gives a stable, bounded route label for logs and metrics.

readings.hint: Count how many distinct values the label could take across all users.
readings.introduction: Every Gin route is a template stored in a radix tree. The router decides which handler runs, what c.Param returns and whether the client gets a redirect instead of your handler. Most routing bugs are not in handler code: they are a trailing slash, an encoded slash or two templates that cannot share a prefix. Learn the matching rules once and those bugs become predictable.
readings.nuance: FullPath is the registered pattern, so /users/1 and /users/2 share one series; it is empty when no route matched, so unmatched requests need their own fixed label.
readings.objective: Declare Gin route templates with :param and *wildcard, predict how slashes and escapes resolve, and label metrics with c.FullPath().
readings.question: A metrics middleware needs a low-cardinality route label. What does c.FullPath() give it?
readings.reviewAnswer: The matched route template, such as /users/:id

sections.body: A named parameter such as :id matches exactly one non-empty path segment: it stops at the next slash and never matches an empty string. A catch-all such as *path must be the last element of the template and captures everything after its position, including the leading slash. There are no regular expressions and no types in the template, so /users/:id accepts "42", "abc" and "-1" alike; turning the string into a number or a UUID is the handler's job. A static segment registered next to a parameter wins when it matches exactly, which is why /users/new and /users/:id can coexist in Gin v1.12.0.
sections.title: A route is a template matched segment by segment

sections.body: The program registers four templates on one engine and sends nine requests. Each handler prints the matched template and every parameter in path order, so you can see what the router decided rather than what you expected. The last request goes to a second engine with UseRawPath enabled to show why one encoded character changes the outcome.
sections.title: Watch the router resolve real paths
sections.walkthrough: describe prints c.FullPath() and ranges over c.Params, which preserves path order. /users/new hits the static route, not :id. The catch-all keeps the leading slash, so /files/ yields path="/". /users/42/ never reaches a handler: RedirectTrailingSlash answers 301 with Location /users/42. /users/ is a 404 because :id cannot be empty. /users/a%2Fb is a 404 on the default engine because Gin routes on the decoded URL.Path, where %2F has become a real slash and splits the segment. With UseRawPath the router matches the encoded form and UnescapePathValues hands the handler id="a/b".

sections.body: Two templates cannot put different wildcards at the same position, and a catch-all cannot share its level with anything else. Gin enforces this when the route is added, by panicking, so a conflicting route table never serves a single request. Treat that panic as a design signal: either the URLs describe different resources and need different prefixes, or one handler should own the position and branch on the value. Registering the same method and path twice also panics with "handlers are already registered".
sections.title: Conflicts fail at startup, which is the good news
sections.walkthrough: This fragment is not compiled; show stands for any handler. The messages are the start of the v1.12.0 panic text. The first pair fails because :id and :name compete for the same segment, even though the second template is longer. The second and third pairs fail because *path claims the whole remainder of /files/ or /assets/, leaving no room for :id or readme. The last line fails on its own: nothing may follow a catch-all. Because these are panics at registration, a test that only calls newRouter() catches them.

sections.body: Three engine flags decide what happens to paths that almost match. RedirectTrailingSlash is on by default: GET requests get a 301, other methods a 307 so the body and method survive, and the query string is kept. The redirect is written before the handler chain runs, so your logging and metrics middleware never see it; if a client keeps hitting /users/42/, only the proxy log will show the extra round trips. It also honors an X-Forwarded-Prefix request header, sanitized to letters, digits, '/' and '-'. RedirectFixedPath is off by default; when enabled it cleans ../ and // and does a case-insensitive lookup, so /USERS/AbC redirects to /users/AbC with the parameter's case preserved. RemoveExtraSlash cleans the path before lookup and serves it directly, without a redirect. For browser-facing pages the redirects are friendly. For a machine API, a 404 on the non-canonical path can be the better contract: it fails loudly in the client's tests instead of costing a hidden round trip on every call.
sections.code:
r := gin.New()
// Defaults in v1.12.0, written out so a reviewer sees the policy.
r.RedirectTrailingSlash = true // /users/42/ -> 301 (GET) or 307 (other methods)
r.RedirectFixedPath = false    // true: /USERS//42 -> 301 /users/42
r.RemoveExtraSlash = false     // true: //users//42 is served as /users/42, no redirect
r.UseRawPath = false           // true: match on URL.RawPath when Go recorded one
r.UseEscapedPath = false       // true: match on URL.EscapedPath(); overrides UseRawPath
r.UnescapePathValues = true    // with raw or escaped matching, decode param values
sections.title: Trailing slashes, case and doubled slashes
sections.walkthrough: This fragment sets every flag to its v1.12.0 default so the routing policy is visible in code review. UseEscapedPath is new in v1.12.0 and takes precedence over UseRawPath. Set these fields before the engine serves traffic: they are plain struct fields read on every request without locking, so changing them later is a data race.

sections.body: Go's url.URL stores both a decoded Path and, only when the client's encoding differs from the default one, a RawPath. A path such as /users/caf%C3%A9 has no RawPath, because that is exactly how Go would encode it, so it matches /users/:id and yields "café" with or without UseRawPath. /users/a%2Fb does record a RawPath. If identifiers can legitimately contain a slash, enable UseRawPath (or UseEscapedPath) and keep UnescapePathValues on, then validate the decoded value: a parameter that may contain '/' or '..' must never be joined into a file path or an upstream URL. If identifiers cannot contain a slash, the default 404 is the safer behavior.
sections.title: Encoded slashes and raw paths

sections.body: c.FullPath() returns the registered template, such as /users/:id, and an empty string when nothing matched. That makes it the right label for request counters and latency histograms: /users/1 and /users/2 share one series. Labeling with c.Request.URL.Path creates a new time series per user, per typo and per scanner probe, which is how a metrics backend runs out of memory. Pin the routing contract with a table test of path, expected status, expected template and expected parameters, including one trailing-slash case, one empty-segment case and one encoded-slash case.
sections.title: Label metrics with FullPath and test with a table
sections.walkthrough: This helper is a fragment for your own metrics middleware: call it after c.Next() so the value reflects the matched route. An empty FullPath means the router found no handler, which covers 404 and 405 responses; collapsing them into one unmatched label keeps the cardinality bounded no matter what paths clients invent.

readings.takeaway: A :param is one non-empty segment and a *wildcard is the rest of the path; Gin rejects conflicting templates at boot, answers near-misses with redirects before middleware runs, and c.FullPath() gives the low-cardinality route label.
readings.title: Path parameters in Gin: :param takes one segment, *wildcard takes the rest, conflicts panic at boot
wrongAnswers: The request path after Gin decodes percent-escapes
The path plus query string, normalized to lowercase

cautions: A '+' in a query string is a space, so +7 does not parse as an integer.
Form parse errors are swallowed by the helpers unless you call ParseForm yourself.
designGuide.cost: A small helper per parameter type and a table test; the alternative is declarative binding, covered later, which trades visibility for brevity.
strengths: GetQuery and GetPostForm make absent and empty explicit.
One contract-style message per parameter stays stable across refactors.

readings.hint: Compare what GetQuery reports for ?limit= and for a request without limit.
readings.introduction: Every query or form value reaches your handler as a string that may be missing, empty, repeated or malformed. Gin offers several helpers that look interchangeable but answer different questions. Choosing the wrong one turns limit=abc into limit 0, or a deliberately empty field into a default the client never asked for.
readings.nuance: DefaultQuery is built on GetQuery, which returns ok=true for ?limit=, so the handler receives "" and must decide whether empty is an error.
readings.objective: Read query and form values with the Gin helper that matches the case, convert them with strconv and reject bad input with a clear 400.
readings.question: When does c.DefaultQuery("limit", "20") return "20" instead of a value from the request?
readings.reviewAnswer: Only when the key is absent, not when its value is empty

sections.body: For any key a request can be in one of four states: absent, present but empty, present and valid, or present and invalid. c.Query collapses the first two into "". c.GetQuery returns the value plus a boolean that is true even for ?q= and for a bare ?q. c.DefaultQuery substitutes its default only when the key is absent. The form helpers PostForm, GetPostForm and DefaultPostForm follow the same rules for the request body. Decide for each parameter what absent and empty mean, then pick the helper that can express that decision.
sections.title: Four states hide behind one string

sections.body: The program implements GET /search with a required q, a bounded limit, repeatable tag values and a filter map, plus POST /notes reading a URL-encoded form. Nine requests cover the default path, three kinds of bad limit, a present-but-empty q, the full happy path, an unknown filter key and the two form cases.
sections.title: A search endpoint and a form endpoint
sections.walkthrough: intQuery returns the default only when the key is absent; a present value must parse and fall in range, otherwise the client gets one message that states the contract. limit=+7 fails because '+' in a query string decodes to a space, so strconv.Atoi sees " 7". q= is present, so GetQuery reports ok and the TrimSpace check rejects it. QueryArray collects repeated tag values in order and returns nil when there are none, which JSON renders as null. QueryMap turns filter[status]=open into a map, and the loop rejects keys outside the allowlist. The last request sends priority= explicitly, so DefaultPostForm returns "" instead of "normal" and the switch rejects it.

sections.body: When a key repeats, GetQuery and Query return the first value and QueryArray returns all of them. QueryMap and PostFormMap read bracket keys such as filter[status]; the result is a Go map, so never let its iteration order reach output or logic that must be stable (encoding/json sorts map keys, which is why the program's output is deterministic). A malformed escape such as %zz is dropped by Go's query parser and Gin does not surface the error, so the key simply looks absent. Forms have a second trap: PostForm reads only the parsed body, never the query string, and Gin's form cache logs a parse failure only in debug mode. A truncated or oversized body therefore shows up as missing fields. When that difference matters, parse explicitly first.
sections.title: Repeated, bracketed and malformed keys
sections.walkthrough: This fragment shows the explicit parse step. Request.ParseForm reads URL-encoded bodies and the query string and returns the first error it meets, including an invalid escape or a body cut off by http.MaxBytesReader. After it succeeds Gin's helpers reuse the parsed values, because ParseForm does not parse twice. GetPostForm still looks only at Request.PostForm, the body values.

sections.body: strconv.Atoi accepts an optional sign and leading zeros, so "+7", "007" and "-1" parse, while " 5", "1e3" and "0x10" are syntax errors and "99999999999999999999" fails with strconv.ErrRange. Use strconv.ParseInt(raw, 10, 32) when the value must fit an int32 column. Do not echo the Go error text to clients: it describes your implementation, not your contract. A message such as "limit must be an integer between 1 and 100" tells a caller exactly how to fix the request and stays stable when you refactor. Use 400 Bad Request for malformed query parameters and keep the error body shape the same across endpoints.
sections.title: strconv is strict; your error message should be too

sections.body: A limit decides how many rows the database reads, how much JSON the server encodes and how long the response holds a connection, so it needs a ceiling as well as a default. An offset needs one too: OFFSET 100000 still makes most databases walk 100000 rows, which is why deep pagination usually moves to a cursor. Cap repeated values, because each tag tends to become another predicate, and allowlist map keys, because filter keys are often mapped to column names and must never be interpolated into SQL. Rejecting out-of-range values surfaces client bugs early; clamping is friendlier for interactive UIs, but if you clamp, echo the effective limit as the program does so the client can see it. Test each parameter as a table: absent, empty, non-numeric, below and above the bounds, '+' and '%2B', repeated, malformed escape and unknown map key. The binding-sources lesson later in this course shows how ShouldBindQuery with form tags and default= values expresses the same rules declaratively.
sections.title: Bound every parameter that sizes the work

readings.takeaway: Use GetQuery or GetPostForm when absent and empty mean different things, parse numbers with strconv and a stated range, and give every limit-style parameter a default, a ceiling and a clear 400 message.
readings.title: Query strings and forms in Gin: tell absent from empty, parse numbers strictly, bound every limit
wrongAnswers: Whenever the value is empty or fails to parse
Whenever the key is absent or its value is empty

cautions: A late group.Use silently skips earlier routes and subgroups.
Group middleware never runs for 404, 405 or trailing-slash redirects.
designGuide.cost: One table test over r.Routes() and the discipline to pass middleware to Group; nothing at request time beyond the copied chain.
strengths: Prefixes and shared middleware are declared once per API area.
Versions can coexist and be retired independently by prefix.

readings.hint: Think about the moment at which a route's handler chain is assembled.
readings.introduction: r.Group("/api/v1") looks like a folder that routes live in, with middleware guarding the door. It is really a registration helper: when you add a route, Gin copies the group's prefix and handler list into that route, and the group plays no part when requests arrive. That one fact explains the most common group bug and tells you how to test for it.
readings.nuance: Registering a route or creating a subgroup copies the group's handlers at that moment; a later Use appends to the group's slice but cannot reach chains that were already copied.
readings.objective: Organize a Gin API into nested, versioned groups with scoped middleware and prove with r.Routes() that every route has the protection you intended.
readings.question: A team calls v1.Use(auth) after registering some v1 routes and creating v1.Group("/admin"). Which routes does auth protect?
readings.reviewAnswer: Only for routes and subgroups created after the call

sections.body: A RouterGroup holds a base path and a slice of handlers. Group(path, middleware...) returns a new group whose handlers are a fresh copy of the parent's plus the ones you pass. Registering GET or POST on a group joins the paths and copies the group's handlers in front of your handler, and the resulting chain is stored with the route in the router tree. At request time Gin finds the route and runs that stored chain; it never asks which group the route came from. Nesting therefore composes cleanly: /api/v1/admin inherits everything /api/v1 had at the moment the admin group was created, plus its own middleware.
sections.title: A group is a prefix plus a copied handler list

sections.body: The program builds a public health check, a v1 group with authentication, an admin subgroup that also requires a role, and a v2 group that changes the response shape. main then lists every route with r.Routes(), calls each one without credentials and labels it, before exercising the authenticated paths.
sections.title: Two versions, an admin subgroup and a route-table test
sections.walkthrough: Middleware is passed to Group itself, so it is in place before any route is added. requireToken stores the role with c.Set; requireRole reads it, so the admin chain is requireToken, requireRole("admin"), adminStats in that order. r.Routes() returns method, path and the name of the final handler; the order is not documented, so the program sorts it. Each route is called with its :id replaced by 1 and no Authorization header. Anything that does not answer 401 must be on the public allowlist, or it prints OPEN BY MISTAKE. v1 and v2 share the users slice but render different JSON, and the user token gets 403 from the admin subgroup while the admin token succeeds.

sections.body: group.Use appends to that group's slice. Routes registered earlier already hold their own copy of the chain, and subgroups created earlier hold theirs, so neither gains the new middleware. The failure is silent: the code reads as if the whole /v1 tree is authenticated, the server starts, and the earlier routes answer anyone. Passing middleware as arguments to Group, as the program does, makes the order impossible to get wrong. If you must call Use, call it on the line right after creating the group and before any route or subgroup.
sections.code:
api := r.Group("/api")
v1 := api.Group("/v1")
v1.GET("/export", exportAll)    // chain copied now: no auth
admin := v1.Group("/admin")     // chain copied now: no auth
v1.Use(requireToken)            // appends to v1's own slice only
v1.GET("/users", listUsersV1)   // protected
admin.GET("/stats", adminStats) // NOT protected
sections.title: Use after registration protects nothing that came before
sections.walkthrough: This fragment shows the bug, not a pattern to copy. /api/v1/export and /api/v1/admin/stats were wired from v1's chain before requireToken was appended, so both serve unauthenticated requests; only /api/v1/users is protected. The route-table test from the program would print OPEN BY MISTAKE for both, which is why that test exists.

sections.body: A v2 group is the place for breaking changes to the HTTP contract: renamed fields, a pagination envelope, stricter validation. Keep both versions as thin adapters over the same application service so a bug fix lands once, and let each group own only its request parsing and response shape. Retire v1 deliberately: label metrics by c.FullPath() so you can see which v1 routes still get traffic, announce the end date with a Sunset response header (RFC 8594) set by a middleware on the v1 group, and delete the group only when its traffic is gone. Versioning by path prefix is the simplest scheme to route, cache and log; header-based versioning is possible but every proxy, cache key and log query then has to know about the header.
sections.title: Versions side by side, one core underneath

sections.body: Group middleware runs only for routes registered through that group. A request for /api/v1/typo matches no route, so Gin answers with its 404 chain, which contains only engine-level middleware from r.Use; the same is true for 405 responses, and trailing-slash redirects run no middleware at all. An unauthenticated client therefore gets 404 for unknown paths and 401 for real ones, which is normal but worth knowing when you reason about route enumeration. r.Routes() reports only the last handler of each chain, so you cannot inspect middleware statically; test behavior instead, as the program does. Give handlers names: a named function shows as main.listUsersV1, while an anonymous one appears as something like main.main.func3, which makes a route-table diff useless in review. Run the route-table test in CI so a newly added route without the expected protection fails the build.
sections.title: What a group cannot see, and what to test

readings.takeaway: Pass middleware to Group before registering routes, keep versions as thin adapters over one core, and assert the protection of every entry in r.Routes() with requests rather than trusting how the code reads.
readings.title: Gin route groups: prefixes and middleware are copied at registration, so test the route table
wrongAnswers: Every route under /v1, because groups are resolved per request
Every route registered on v1, but none of its subgroups

cautions: Marshal errors and repeated renders leave the first status in place.
AsciiJSON mis-encodes characters above U+FFFF.
designGuide.cost: One DTO type and mapping function per resource, plus contract tests; mapping is cheap compared with an accidental data leak.
strengths: A DTO makes every published field a reviewed decision.
c.JSON output is HTML-safe and has a stable Content-Type.

readings.hint: Check which kinds of values omitempty treats as empty.
readings.introduction: The bytes a handler writes are a public contract: field names, which fields exist, how characters are escaped, the Content-Type and the status. Gin has five JSON renderers that look interchangeable and are not, and c.JSON will happily publish every field of whatever struct you hand it, including the ones you add next year.
readings.nuance: omitempty checks false, 0, nil and zero length, and a struct is none of those, so the zero time renders as 0001-01-01T00:00:00Z; omitzero consults the IsZero method instead.
readings.objective: Choose between c.JSON, PureJSON, IndentedJSON, SecureJSON and AsciiJSON by their exact output, set status codes deliberately and render a response DTO with correct omitempty and omitzero tags.
readings.question: A DTO field is CreatedAt time.Time `json:"created_at,omitempty"` and the value is zero. What does encoding/json do?
readings.reviewAnswer: It is still encoded; omitzero drops it via IsZero

sections.body: All of Gin's JSON renderers start from the configured codec, which is encoding/json unless the binary is built with the jsoniter, go_json or sonic tags. encoding/json exports every exported field, using the Go field name when there is no tag. Rendering a storage struct therefore couples the API to the schema: renaming a column renames a JSON key, and adding a field such as PasswordHash or an internal flag publishes it immediately. A separate response type, a DTO, is the boundary where you decide what leaves the process.
sections.title: Rendering is where internal state leaks

sections.body: The program renders the same small value with each JSON renderer, then contrasts a storage struct with its DTO, and finishes with two cases where Gin drops the body. Newlines in bodies are printed as \n so you can see exactly where each renderer adds one.
sections.title: Ten responses side by side
sections.walkthrough: c.JSON escapes <, > and & as \u003c, \u003e and \u0026 and leaves the UTF-8 é alone. PureJSON writes the characters literally and ends with \n, because it uses a json.Encoder. AsciiJSON also rewrites é as \u00e9 and sends Content-Type application/json without a charset. IndentedJSON uses four spaces. SecureJSON prefixes while(1); only to the array. /leaky shows Go field names and the password hash; the DTO uses snake_case tags, drops the hash, keeps the zero updated_at because omitempty never omits a struct, and drops deleted_at because omitzero asks time.Time.IsZero. The 204 body is discarded. The NaN cannot be marshaled, so Gin records the error in c.Errors, writes nothing, and the client receives 200 with an empty body.

sections.body: Use c.JSON by default: its HTML escaping makes the output safe to embed in a page and it adds no trailing newline. PureJSON is for clients that need literal characters, such as a payload that is signed or compared byte for byte; never embed its output in HTML. IndentedJSON costs bytes and CPU on every request, so keep it for debugging endpoints. SecureJSON defends against JSON hijacking in very old browsers by prefixing top-level arrays (the check is literally output that starts with [ and ends with ]); r.SecureJsonPrefix changes the prefix, and note that the method's doc comment says while(1), while the v1.12.0 default is while(1);. Returning an object at the top level avoids the issue and leaves room for pagination fields. AsciiJSON rewrites each non-ASCII rune with the format \u%04x, so characters above U+FFFF, which includes most emoji, come out as \u plus five hex digits, which a JSON parser reads as a different character followed by a digit. Do not use it for user-generated text.
sections.title: Choose a renderer by its exact bytes

sections.body: c.Status(code) records the status; with no body written, the response goes out empty when the chain finishes. For 1xx, 204 and 304, c.JSON writes the Content-Type header but discards the body, so c.Status(http.StatusNoContent) states the intent more honestly. c.Data(code, contentType, bytes) sends pre-encoded bytes and, since v1.12.0, sets Content-Length. In middleware, c.AbortWithStatusJSON stops the chain and answers in one call. Two failures are silent. A marshal error, from NaN, an infinity, a channel or a cycle, leaves a 200 with an empty body plus an entry in c.Errors, so an error middleware must check c.Errors as the errors-testing lesson does. A second render after the first one has written appends its body to the first and cannot change the status, so one function must own the response.
sections.title: Status codes and the bodies Gin drops

sections.body: omitempty omits false, 0, "", nil pointers and interfaces, and slices, maps or strings of length zero; it never omits a struct, so a zero time.Time renders as 0001-01-01T00:00:00Z. omitzero, added in Go 1.24, omits a field when its type's IsZero method returns true or, without such a method, when the value is the zero value. That makes it right for time.Time and for value structs, but a non-nil empty slice is not a zero value, so omitzero keeps [] where omitempty drops it. With both options the field is omitted if either rule applies. Decide per field whether clients should see absent, null, zero or empty, and write that down in the tag.
sections.title: omitempty versus omitzero in a DTO
sections.walkthrough: This fragment annotates a pagination DTO. A nil Items slice encodes as null, which many clients mishandle, so initialize it to an empty slice. NextCursor disappears on the last page. Total with omitzero disappears when it is 0, which is wrong if zero is a meaningful count, so think before tagging numbers. Generated relies on time.Time.IsZero, which is exactly what omitzero consults.

sections.body: For each endpoint assert the status, the Content-Type and the body. Decode the body into map[string]any and assert that sensitive keys such as password_hash are absent, because a struct-to-struct comparison cannot notice an extra field. Keep a golden file per DTO for contract review, and add one test that marshals every DTO with representative values, including floats from calculations, so a NaN fails in CI rather than as an empty 200 in production. If the JSON codec is swapped with build tags, run the same tests under that build.
sections.title: Test the bytes, not just the status

readings.takeaway: Render DTOs with explicit tags, use c.JSON unless a renderer's exact bytes are required, and remember that a marshal error or a second render does not change the status already chosen.
readings.title: Gin JSON responses: know what each renderer writes and return a DTO, never your storage model
wrongAnswers: It omits the field because the time is the zero value
It encodes null because zero times are treated as nil

cautions: ShouldBind falls back to form binding for unknown content types.
ShouldBindBodyWith buffers the whole body; cap its size first.
designGuide.cost: A few small structs per endpoint and one extra in-memory copy of the body when it must be decoded twice.
strengths: Each error names the source that was wrong.
default= options keep simple query defaults declarative.

readings.hint: Look at what binding.Uri does right after it maps the path parameters.
readings.introduction: A single request carries input in four places: path parameters, the query string, headers and the body. Gin has a binder and a struct tag for each, and they compose well as long as you respect two rules the API does not advertise. Every binder validates the entire struct it fills, and a request body can be read only once unless you ask Gin to keep a copy.
readings.nuance: BindUri maps only uri tags and then runs the validator on the entire struct, so the still-empty Title fails required before ShouldBindJSON has had a chance to fill it.
readings.objective: Bind each request source with its own Gin binder and tag, predict what content-type-driven ShouldBind reads, and decode one body twice with ShouldBindBodyWithJSON.
readings.question: A struct has a uri-tagged ID and a json-tagged Title, both binding:"required". Why does ShouldBindUri fail on a valid request?
readings.reviewAnswer: Each binder validates the whole struct, not its own tags
readings.reviewPrompt: Why one struct per binding source?

sections.body: ShouldBindUri fills fields tagged uri from c.Params. ShouldBindQuery fills form-tagged fields from the URL query only. ShouldBindHeader fills header-tagged fields, canonicalizing the tag with textproto.CanonicalMIMEHeaderKey, so header:"x-request-id" works. ShouldBindJSON decodes the body into json-tagged fields. After mapping, every binder runs the validator, which reads the binding tag. The Should variants return the error and leave the response to you; the Bind variants abort with a bare 400 and, in v1.12.0, no body at all, which is rarely the error contract an API wants. A form tag can carry a default, as in form:"limit,default=20", which applies only when the key is absent.
sections.title: Four sources, four tags, one binder each

sections.body: The program defines one small struct per source and wires them into five handlers: a list endpoint with path, query and header input, a PATCH that needs an If-Match header, a create endpoint that accepts JSON or a form through ShouldBind, and two webhook handlers that read the same body twice, one correctly and one naively.
sections.title: Path, query, headers, body and a webhook
sections.walkthrough: The first request gets limit 20 and sort created from the default= options. limit=0 is present, so the default does not apply and min=1 rejects it. core.v2 fails alphanum in the path. /notes/abc fails before validation because strconv cannot parse an int64. The PATCH without If-Match fails header validation, and the one with it echoes the quoted entity tag. ShouldBind picks the JSON or form binder from Content-Type, so both create requests succeed. /webhooks decodes the envelope, switches on its type, then decodes the full payload from the cached bytes. /webhooks-naive calls ShouldBindJSON twice; the first call drained the body, so the second sees EOF.

sections.body: It is tempting to describe a whole request in one struct with uri, json and header tags side by side. Each binder maps only its own tag, but binding.Uri, binding.Query, binding.Header and the body binders all validate the complete struct afterwards. A required body field is therefore still empty when ShouldBindUri runs, and the call fails on a perfectly valid request. Separate structs per source avoid the problem and also make the error message honest: you know which source was wrong. If you insist on one struct, the only arrangement that works is to put binding rules solely on the fields filled by the binder you call last, which quietly gives up validation for every other source.
sections.title: Why one struct per source
sections.walkthrough: This fragment is the anti-pattern, with the v1.12.0 error text as a comment. ShouldBindUri sets ID correctly, then validation reaches Title, which is empty because the JSON body has not been decoded yet, and required fails. Swapping the call order only moves the failure: ShouldBindJSON would then complain about ID.

sections.body: ShouldBind asks binding.Default(method, contentType) for a binder. For GET it always returns the form binder, so a JSON body on a GET is ignored and only the query string is read. For other methods the media type, with parameters such as charset stripped, selects JSON, XML, YAML, TOML, protobuf, MessagePack, BSON or multipart. Anything else, including a missing Content-Type or text/plain, falls back to the form binder, which reads Request.Form: the URL-encoded body merged with the query string, body values first. A client can therefore supply a field through the query string of a POST. If an endpoint accepts only JSON, call ShouldBindJSON and answer 415 for other content types instead of letting the fallback guess.
sections.title: Content-Type decides what ShouldBind reads

sections.body: Request.Body is a stream; once a decoder has consumed it, the next read returns EOF. ShouldBindBodyWith(obj, binding.JSON), or the shortcut ShouldBindBodyWithJSON, reads the whole body with io.ReadAll on first use, stores the bytes in c.Keys under gin.BodyBytesKey and decodes from that copy on every later call. That is what an envelope-then-payload webhook needs. It only works with body binders such as JSON, XML, YAML, TOML and Plain, not with the form binder, and once one call has cached the body every other read in that request must use the BodyWith variants too. Because the whole body is buffered in memory, put http.MaxBytesReader in front of it as described in the binding-limits lesson; that lesson also covers when to reject unknown fields.
sections.title: Reading the body twice without losing it

sections.body: Write table cases per source rather than per endpoint: a path value of the wrong type, a query key that is absent versus present with a zero value, a header in unusual case, a body with no Content-Type, an empty body, and a second read of the same body. Assert both the status and which source the error names, because a test that only checks for 400 cannot tell a header mistake from a body mistake. The next lesson turns validator errors into a stable field-level JSON response.
sections.title: Test each source on its own

readings.takeaway: Give each request source its own struct and binder, call ShouldBindJSON when only JSON is acceptable, and use ShouldBindBodyWithJSON behind a size limit when one body must be decoded twice.
readings.title: Gin binding sources: bind path, query, headers and body separately, and cache the body to read it twice
wrongAnswers: ShouldBindUri also reads the JSON body and finds it empty
Gin forbids mixing uri and json tags in one struct

cautions: Register methods are not thread-safe; finish them before serving.
Without dive, struct elements of a slice are never validated.
designGuide.cost: One setup function, one error mapper shared by all handlers and a table test per rule; registration is global, so tag names need care.
strengths: Domain rules live next to the DTO and run for every binder.
Field, rule and param objects stay stable across refactors.

readings.hint: Remove dive from the program's Items tag and send the invalid SKU again.
readings.introduction: Gin's binding tags cover shape: required, lengths, ranges, enumerations. Real input also has domain rules, such as a SKU format or an address that is required unless the customer picks the order up. Gin's validator accepts both kinds, but the default error text names Go structs and fields, which makes a poor API. This lesson adds the rules and a response format you can keep stable.
readings.nuance: Without dive the validator checks only the slice itself, such as required and min; dive tells it to descend into every element, applying the tags after dive and each struct element's own tags.
readings.objective: Register a custom tag and a struct-level rule on Gin's validator, validate slice elements with dive and convert validator errors into a stable field-level JSON response.
readings.question: Items []line has binding:"required,min=1" and every line struct has its own binding tags. What does adding dive change?
readings.reviewAnswer: It makes the validator visit and validate each element
readings.reviewPrompt: What does dive do in a slice tag?

sections.body: binding.Validator is a package-level StructValidator. The default implementation lazily creates a go-playground/validator v10 instance with its tag name set to binding, and Engine() returns it as any. Type-assert it to *validator.Validate and you can register custom tags, struct-level rules and a tag-name function. Because the instance is global, everything you register applies to every binder in the process: ShouldBindJSON, ShouldBindQuery, ShouldBindUri and the rest. Give custom tags specific names such as sku rather than code, so two packages cannot collide.
sections.title: Gin's validator is a shared go-playground instance

sections.body: The program registers a sku tag, a struct-level rule for the address and a tag-name function, then posts five orders: a valid one, one with four separate problems, one with no items, one with a wrongly typed field and one that is not JSON at all.
sections.title: An order endpoint with domain rules
sections.walkthrough: RegisterTagNameFunc makes errors report JSON names, so Namespace() yields order.items[1].sku and the handler strips the leading type name. The sku function is an ordinary predicate over the field. The struct-level rule reports its own tag, required_unless_pickup, through ReportError. The second request produces four errors in struct order with element errors by index and the struct-level error last. {"items":[]} passes required, because a non-nil empty slice is not missing, and fails min=1. "qty":"2" never reaches validation: encoding/json returns an UnmarshalTypeError whose Field is items.0.qty, which wirePath rewrites as items[0].qty. A truncated body is reported as malformed JSON.

sections.body: The validator is safe for concurrent validation, but its Register methods are documented as not thread-safe: they must all run before any validation. Call your setup from main before the server starts, or wrap it in sync.OnceValue when tests construct routers concurrently. The type assertion is worth checking rather than ignoring: if someone installs a different binding.Validator, registration should fail at startup instead of silently doing nothing. Unit-test a custom tag directly with Validate.Var, which runs one tag against one value without a request.
sections.title: Register once, before serving
sections.walkthrough: This fragment shows the startup guard. sync.OnceValue runs setupValidation exactly once and returns the same error to every caller, so a broken registration fails every router construction consistently. Validate.Var is the cheapest place to test the edges of the SKU pattern: case, length and separator.

sections.body: Rules before dive apply to the collection, rules after dive apply to each element. Without dive the validator checks only the slice itself and never visits the elements, even when they are structs with their own binding tags, so items:[{"sku":"abc"}] would pass. Nested struct fields are validated without dive; a nil pointer to a struct is skipped unless the pointer field itself is required. Watch required on non-strings: on a slice it rejects only a nil value, so pair it with min=1, and on an int it rejects 0, which is why qty uses min=1 and reports a meaningful rule. If 0 must be distinguishable from an absent field, use a pointer such as *int.
sections.title: dive, required and the zero value

sections.body: err.Error() on ValidationErrors produces text such as Key: 'order.Items[1].SKU' Error:Field validation for 'SKU' failed on the 'sku' tag. It exposes Go type names and changes when you rename a struct. Return a list of objects instead: field as the wire path with JSON names and [i] indices, rule as the tag name, which is a short machine-readable code, and param for bounds such as min=1 or len=8. Clients can map rule to a localized message, or you can use the validator's translation support on the server. Type errors from encoding/json happen before validation, so map them into the same shape. Use 422 for well-formed input that breaks a rule and 400 for input that cannot be decoded, or one status for both, but keep the convention identical across endpoints.
sections.title: A stable field-error contract

sections.body: Table tests should hit both sides of every boundary: SKU in lower case or with three digits, quantities 0, 1, 99 and 100, zero, one, twenty and twenty-one items, a fourth coupon, a seven-character coupon, pickup false with a blank address. Assert the exact JSON body, since the order of errors is deterministic. Keep business rules that need current state, such as stock levels or coupon ownership, out of validators: they belong in the use case, after validation, as the binding-limits lesson argues.
sections.title: Test the rules at their edges

readings.takeaway: Register custom tags and struct rules on binding.Validator once at startup, dive into collections explicitly, and translate ValidationErrors into field, rule and param objects that use wire names.
readings.title: Custom validators in Gin: register domain rules once and return field errors clients can rely on
wrongAnswers: It stops validation at the first failing element
It applies the slice's own rules again to nested slices

cautions: c.Value ignores non-string keys stored with c.Set.
With Recovery outermost, panicking requests leave no access-log line.
designGuide.cost: A few small functions and one ordering decision per engine; the per-request overhead is a slice index and a map write per value.
strengths: Post-Next code observes status, errors and abort state for every request.
Typed keys and accessors make request values collision-free and explicit.

readings.hint: Look at which loop invokes the handlers and when it stops.
readings.introduction: Gin middleware is an ordinary handler that happens to run before others in the same chain. Most middleware bugs come from a wrong mental model of that chain: expecting Abort to return, expecting a middleware without c.Next to stop the request, or reading a status before the handler has chosen it. This lesson builds four realistic middleware functions and traces exactly what runs.
readings.nuance: Gin's top-level c.Next loop keeps advancing the index after each handler returns; only Abort moves the index past the end, so Next matters only for code that must run afterwards.
readings.objective: Write Gin middleware that runs code after c.Next, stops the chain with Abort and return, shares typed values through c.Set and c.Get, and is ordered so logs see the final outcome.
readings.question: A middleware sets a header and returns without calling c.Next(). What happens to the rest of the chain?
readings.reviewAnswer: The chain still continues when the middleware returns

sections.body: For a matched route Gin stores one slice of handlers: engine middleware from r.Use, then group middleware, then the handlers passed to the route, in registration order. Serving a request calls c.Next once, which runs the slice in a loop. When a handler calls c.Next itself, the remaining handlers run inside that call and control comes back afterwards; when it returns without calling c.Next, the outer loop simply continues with the next handler. So c.Next is needed only when you want code to run after the rest of the chain. c.Abort sets the chain index to a sentinel so every loop stops, and c.IsAborted reports whether that happened. Abort does not return from the current function and does not undo anything already written.
sections.title: The chain is one loop over a slice

sections.body: The program registers an access log and a request-ID middleware globally, an authentication guard on two routes and a role guard on one of them. Each middleware appends to a trace, so every response line shows which functions ran and in what order. The access-log lines printed at the end show what the outermost middleware can observe after c.Next.
sections.title: An access log, a request ID and two guards
sections.walkthrough: accessLog wraps everything: "log>" is recorded before c.Next and "<log" after it, even for the aborted requests and the 404, because aborting stops later handlers but returns control to earlier ones. requestID never calls c.Next, yet the chain continues. requireUser aborts with 401 and returns, so neither "me" nor the role check runs. On the DELETE with a member token the role guard aborts with 403. After c.Next the log reads the request ID set by an inner middleware, the template from FullPath, the final status and IsAborted. The unmatched request runs only engine middleware, which is why its trace has no guards.

sections.body: After c.Next returns, c.Writer.Status() holds the status the chain chose, which is 200 if nobody set one, so a handler that writes nothing still logs as 200. c.Writer.Written() and c.Writer.Size() tell you whether a body was written; Size is -1 when nothing was, because Gin flushes the final header only after the whole chain returns. c.Errors holds errors attached with c.Error. It is too late to change headers once the body is written, so set response headers such as X-Request-Id before c.Next, as requestID does. Panics skip the code after c.Next unless a recovery runs inside you: with accessLog registered before gin.Recovery(), the log sees the 500 that Recovery writes; with the order reversed the log line for a panicking request is simply missing.
sections.title: Code after Next sees the outcome, not the bytes on the wire

sections.body: In v1.12.0 c.Keys is a map[any]any protected by a mutex, and Set, Get and MustGet take a key of type any. Use an unexported key type, as with context.WithValue, so two packages cannot overwrite each other's "user". Wrap reads in a typed accessor such as currentUser. MustGet panics with "key ... does not exist", which is right when a missing value means the route was wired without its guard; use Get and its ok flag for optional values. One trap: *gin.Context implements context.Context, but its Value method looks in Keys only for string keys, so c.Value(userKey) returns nil here and then falls back to the request context only if engine.ContextWithFallback is set. Pass the user to services as an argument, or attach it with c.Request.WithContext. Keys are cleared when the context returns to Gin's pool, so never keep them past the handler; the context-workers lesson covers that boundary.
sections.title: Typed keys for c.Set and c.Get

sections.body: Engine-level middleware runs for every request, including 404 and 405 responses, so it is the place for access logs, metrics, request IDs and recovery. Group middleware suits authentication for an area of the API. Per-route middleware suits authorization and endpoint-specific policies such as a body limit or an idempotency check. Order them so observers wrap actors: logging and metrics outermost, recovery inside them, request ID before anything that logs, authentication before authorization.
sections.code:
r := gin.New()
// Outermost first: the log observes the 500 that Recovery writes.
r.Use(accessLog(logger), gin.Recovery(), requestID(newID))

api := r.Group("/api", requireUser)                        // authentication per area
api.GET("/me", me)                                         // any signed-in user
api.DELETE("/users/:id", requireRole("admin"), deleteUser) // authorization per route
sections.title: Choose where each middleware lives
sections.walkthrough: This fragment shows the layering with placeholder constructors. The access log is outermost so it records every status, including the 500 from a recovered panic. requireUser guards the whole /api group, and requireRole("admin") runs only for the DELETE route, after authentication has stored the user.

sections.body: Build a tiny engine with the middleware under test and a probe handler that records it ran. Assert the status, the headers, whether the probe ran, and what an outer recording middleware observed. Cover every abort path, a panic behind the recovery, and hostile input: a client-supplied X-Request-Id flows into your logs, so cap its length as the program does and restrict its characters before trusting it.
sections.title: Test middleware as part of a chain

readings.takeaway: Call c.Next only when you need to run code afterwards, follow every Abort with return, read the outcome after Next from c.Writer and c.Errors, and share request values through typed keys and accessors.
readings.title: Writing Gin middleware: what c.Next returns to, what Abort does not do, and typed request values
wrongAnswers: The request stops there and the client gets an empty 200
Gin panics because every middleware must call c.Next()

cautions: FormFile reads the whole body before you can inspect the file.
Sniffing checks signatures only; images still need decoding limits.
designGuide.cost: A size cap, a 512-byte sniff and a hash pass per upload, plus a streaming path once files get large.
strengths: Type decisions rest on content, not on client labels.
Generated names remove traversal, collision and overwrite risks.

readings.hint: Read how Request.ParseMultipartForm describes its maxMemory argument.
readings.introduction: An upload is attacker-controlled bytes wrapped in attacker-controlled labels. The filename, the declared Content-Type and the size all come from the client, and so does the number of parts. c.FormFile makes accepting a file one line long, which is exactly why the limits, the type decision and the storage name have to be written deliberately around it.
readings.nuance: MaxMultipartMemory is the maxMemory argument to ParseMultipartForm: the remainder of the file is written to temporary files, so only http.MaxBytesReader actually bounds the request.
readings.objective: Accept a multipart upload in Gin with a hard size cap, decide its type from its content, generate the storage name yourself and test it with a request built by mime/multipart.
readings.question: An engine sets MaxMultipartMemory = 8 << 20 and has no other limit. What does that setting cap when a client uploads a 2 GiB file?
readings.reviewAnswer: Only memory use; larger file parts spill to temp files

sections.body: A handler that calls c.FormFile and then c.SaveUploadedFile(file, "uploads/"+file.Filename) has four separate bugs. Nothing bounds the request, so one client can fill memory or the temp directory. The declared type is trusted, so an HTML page labeled image/png can be served back from your origin and run script there. The client's name decides where the file lands, so uploads overwrite each other or land somewhere unexpected. And SaveUploadedFile creates the parent directory and, in v1.12.0, also chmods it to 0o750 on every call, which can surprise an operator who set permissions on a shared directory.
sections.title: What goes wrong with a naive upload handler

sections.body: The program accepts an avatar, enforces a request cap and a per-file cap, sniffs the first 512 bytes, derives the extension from an allowlist and names the file after its SHA-256. main sends seven requests: six built with mime/multipart, the same encoding a browser uses, including files that lie about their type, and one that is not multipart at all.
sections.title: An avatar endpoint and the requests that probe it
sections.walkthrough: http.MaxBytesReader wraps the body before FormFile parses it, so the 10 KiB file fails with *http.MaxBytesError and a 413, while the 5 KiB file fits the request cap and fails the fh.Size check instead. The PHP script and the HTML page both claim to be images in their part headers, but DetectContentType reports text/plain and text/html and the allowlist rejects them with 415. The first request's filename was ../../avatar.png; mime/multipart already reduced it to avatar.png, and the handler uses it only as display metadata. The stored name is the hash plus the extension chosen by the allowlist. A missing part yields http.ErrMissingFile, and a JSON body fails multipart parsing.

sections.body: Engine.MaxMultipartMemory, 32 MiB by default, is passed to Request.ParseMultipartForm as maxMemory. File parts up to that total stay in memory and the rest spill to temporary files in os.TempDir; non-file fields may use up to another 10 MiB of memory on top. Nothing in it bounds the request, so always wrap the body with http.MaxBytesReader before FormFile, MultipartForm, PostForm or ShouldBind touch it. The cap counts the whole encoded body, including boundaries and other fields, so check fh.Size for the per-file rule. Go also limits a form to 1000 parts by default, adjustable with GODEBUG=multipartmaxparts. http.Server removes the temporary files after the handler returns. Note that FormFile reads the entire body before you see the first byte of the file; for large uploads, stream with Request.MultipartReader instead.
sections.title: MaxMultipartMemory is a buffer size, not a limit
sections.walkthrough: This fragment is a streaming variant for large files; run it in your own environment against real storage. MultipartReader yields parts one at a time without buffering them or creating temp files. bufio.Reader.Peek exposes the first bytes of the avatar part for sniffing without consuming them, so the same reader can then be copied to storage while hashing. The size cap still wraps the body because the client decides how much it sends.

sections.body: http.DetectContentType implements the WHATWG MIME sniffing algorithm over at most 512 bytes and always returns a valid type, falling back to application/octet-stream. Allowlist the sniffed type and derive the extension from the allowlist, never from the filename. Sniffing only checks signatures: a file can start with a PNG header and still be malformed, or be a polyglot that is valid in two formats. For images, also run image.DecodeConfig to bound the pixel dimensions before decoding, since a small file can declare an enormous canvas, and consider re-encoding to strip metadata such as GPS coordinates. When serving uploads back, send the stored type with X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, use Content-Disposition: attachment for anything that is not an image, and prefer a separate domain for user content.
sections.title: Decide the type from the bytes, then constrain how you serve it

sections.body: mime/multipart passes the filename through filepath.Base, as RFC 7578 requires, but that is a platform-dependent cleanup, not a policy. Client names still collide, can contain control characters or lookalike Unicode, can be thousands of bytes long and can carry a misleading extension. Generate the name. A content hash, as in the program, deduplicates identical files and makes retries idempotent, but two users uploading the same file share a name, and a public URL then reveals that a known file exists. crypto/rand.Text returns an unguessable name per upload when that matters. Keep the original name only as length-capped display metadata, store files outside any directory you serve statically, and write through a temporary name followed by a rename so a half-written file never becomes visible.
sections.title: Generate the storage name yourself

sections.body: Build test requests with mime/multipart and a fixed boundary, as main does, so the bodies are deterministic. Cover a missing part, a wrong field name, a request over the cap, a file over its own cap but under the request cap, each kind of disguised content, an empty file and a request that is not multipart. Assert the status and the stored name, and assert that rejected uploads left nothing in storage.
sections.title: Test uploads with real multipart bodies

readings.takeaway: Wrap the body in http.MaxBytesReader before parsing, check fh.Size, choose the type from DetectContentType against an allowlist, and store under a name you generate rather than one the client sent.
readings.title: File uploads in Gin: cap the request, sniff the bytes and never let the client name the file
wrongAnswers: The request size: Gin answers 413 after 8 MiB
The file size: it is truncated to 8 MiB for the handler

cautions: Template errors after c.HTML starts still return 200.
Plain http.FS exposes directory listings through StaticFS.
designGuide.cost: One startup parse, a buffer per buffered page and a cache policy to maintain alongside the build step that fingerprints assets.
strengths: Contextual escaping covers HTML, attributes, URLs and scripts.
Embedded templates and assets ship inside one binary.

readings.hint: Compare the /broken and /broken-buffered responses.
readings.introduction: Gin can render server-side HTML with very little code, and Go's html/template does the hardest part, escaping, for you. What Gin leaves to you are the operational decisions: how templates reach the binary, what happens when a template fails halfway, whether a directory listing is exposed and how long browsers and CDNs may keep each file.
readings.nuance: c.HTML sets the status before executing into the response, so a failure leaves a 200 with an empty or partial page; buffering lets the handler pick the status after execution has succeeded.
readings.objective: Render html/template pages with c.HTML from templates parsed out of an embedded file system, serve embedded static assets with StaticFS and set cache headers per kind of asset.
readings.question: Why does renderPage execute the template into a bytes.Buffer instead of calling c.HTML directly?
readings.reviewAnswer: So a template error can still become a 500, not a 200
readings.reviewPrompt: Why render HTML into a buffer?

sections.body: c.HTML(code, name, data) asks the engine's HTMLRender for the named template and executes it into the response with Content-Type text/html; charset=utf-8. The escaping comes from html/template, which parses the template's HTML structure and escapes each action for the context it appears in: element text, an attribute, a URL, a script or a style. The same string therefore gets different encodings in different places, and none of them can break out of its context. Two rules keep that guarantee: import html/template, never text/template, for HTML, and reserve template.HTML, template.URL and template.JS for content you produced yourself, because those types switch escaping off.
sections.title: html/template escapes by context; Gin only picks the template

sections.body: The program parses two templates from a file system, renders a profile whose display name is an XSS payload, serves two static files through StaticFS with different cache rules and shows what happens when a template is missing, with and without buffered rendering. An fstest.MapFS stands in for embed.FS because go:embed needs files next to the source; both implement fs.FS, so the code is the same.
sections.title: A page, its assets and two failure modes
sections.walkthrough: Funcs is called before ParseFS because a template that mentions asset cannot parse without it. The payload is escaped three ways: as <img in the heading, percent-encoded in the href query and as a quoted JavaScript string with \u003c inside the script. /broken shows the trap: c.HTML has already chosen 200 when the lookup fails, so the client gets an empty 200 page. renderPage executes into a buffer first and turns the same error into a 500. The fingerprinted stylesheet gets a year-long immutable lifetime, the logo five minutes, and the missing file no cache header at all.

sections.body: Gin v1.12.0 offers LoadHTMLGlob, LoadHTMLFiles and LoadHTMLFS(fs http.FileSystem, patterns...). With an embed.FS you would call r.LoadHTMLFS(http.FS(site), "templates/*.html"), which panics through template.Must if a template does not parse. In debug mode all three install a renderer that re-parses on every request, useful for files on disk during development and pointless for embedded ones. Parsing yourself with template.ParseFS and handing the result to SetHTMLTemplate returns an ordinary error and leaves you holding the *template.Template for buffered rendering. All files share one namespace, so if two pages each {{define "content"}}, the last one parsed silently wins. Give blocks unique names, as the program does, or build one template set per page behind a custom render.HTMLRender.
sections.title: Load templates from an embedded file system
sections.walkthrough: This fragment is the production shape; build it in your own module with templates/ and static/ directories next to the source file, which the go:embed line compiles into the binary. It is the program's code with embed.FS in place of fstest.MapFS. Gin calls tmpl.Funcs(engine.FuncMap) inside SetHTMLTemplate, but functions used by templates must already be registered before parsing, which is why funcs is passed to template.New("").Funcs.

sections.body: c.HTML records the status and then executes the template straight into the response writer. If execution fails, Gin appends the error to c.Errors and aborts, but the status is already 200 and any HTML written so far has gone to the client. A missing template yields an empty 200 page; a failure halfway through, for example a method returning an error on a nil field, yields half a page. For pages that must be all-or-nothing, execute into a bytes.Buffer and send it with c.Data, as renderPage does. The cost is holding the page in memory, which is negligible for typical pages and wrong for very large streamed reports.
sections.title: A template error after the status is a silent 200

sections.body: StaticFS("/static", fs) registers GET and HEAD for /static/*filepath. With a plain http.FS, a request for a directory returns an HTML listing of its files. Wrapping the file system in &gin.OnlyFilesFS, which must be a pointer because that is the type Gin checks, turns directory requests into 404s; missing files run the NoRoute handlers or return an empty 404. Files in an embed.FS have a zero modification time, so http.FileServer sends no Last-Modified header, and it never computes an ETag, so browsers cannot revalidate cheaply. Set Cache-Control yourself: a year with immutable for fingerprinted names that change whenever the content does, a short max-age for stable names, and no-cache for HTML. Set the header only after confirming the file exists, as cacheAssets does, so a CDN never stores a 404 for a year.
sections.title: Serve embedded assets with explicit cache rules

sections.body: Execute every page once in a test with representative data, including hostile strings and nil fields. html/template computes its escaping on first execution, so some template errors appear only then, not at parse time. Assert the Content-Type, the escaped forms of the payload in each context, the Cache-Control value per kind of asset, a 404 for a directory and a 500 rather than an empty 200 for a failing page.
sections.title: Test pages and assets like any other response

readings.takeaway: Parse html/template files from an embedded FS at startup, render pages that must not fail halfway through a buffer, disable directory listings with OnlyFilesFS and give each class of asset an explicit Cache-Control.
readings.title: Server-rendered HTML in Gin: embed the templates, trust contextual escaping, cache assets on purpose
wrongAnswers: Because c.HTML does not apply html/template escaping
Because Gin cannot render templates parsed from an FS

cautions: Group middleware, including auth and CORS on a group, never runs for misses.
A wrong 301 is cached by browsers and hard to undo.
designGuide.cost: Two handlers and one flag per engine, plus tests for each miss; the 405 path adds one lookup per method tree on every unmatched request.
strengths: Clients get one JSON error format for hits and misses.
Allow headers tell callers exactly which methods exist.

readings.hint: Gin keeps a separate routing tree for every method; which one does a HEAD request search?
readings.introduction: A Gin engine answers misses on its own: a plain-text 404 for unknown paths and, by default, the same 404 for a known path with the wrong method. API clients that expect JSON errors choke on the text, and a 404 for a wrong method sends whoever is debugging in the wrong direction. A few lines of configuration fix both, and the same lesson applies to redirects: the status code decides whether the method and body survive.
readings.nuance: There is no implicit HEAD fallback in Gin's router, so HEAD /items is a 404, or a 405 with Allow: GET when HandleMethodNotAllowed is on.
readings.objective: Configure NoRoute, NoMethod and HandleMethodNotAllowed for consistent JSON 404 and 405 responses with a correct Allow header, and choose between 301, 302, 303, 307 and 308 for redirects.
readings.question: Does Gin serve HEAD /items from a route registered only with api.GET("/items", ...)?
readings.reviewAnswer: No; register HEAD explicitly, for example with Match
readings.reviewPrompt: Does a GET route answer HEAD?

sections.body: Gin keeps one routing tree per HTTP method and looks only in the tree for the request's method. With HandleMethodNotAllowed at its default of false, PUT /api/items is a 404 even when GET /api/items exists, and the body is the text/plain string "404 page not found". Setting HandleMethodNotAllowed to true makes Gin search the other trees after a miss, and NoRoute and NoMethod let you replace the default bodies with the error format the rest of your API uses.
sections.title: Gin's defaults: plain text, and 404 for wrong methods

sections.body: The program enables 405 handling, installs JSON NoRoute and NoMethod handlers, registers a small items API plus a health route for GET and HEAD, and adds four redirect routes. Thirteen requests cover wrong methods, HEAD, an unknown path, a trailing slash, each redirect code and an attempted open redirect.
sections.title: An API that answers its misses
sections.walkthrough: PUT /api/items finds no PUT route, so Gin checks the other trees, sets Allow: GET, POST and runs NoMethod, which reads that header back into its message. HEAD /api/items is a 405 as well: a GET route does not answer HEAD. /api/health was registered with Match for both methods and answers 200. /api/nothing runs NoRoute. /api/items/ never reaches either handler, because the trailing-slash redirect fires first. GET and POST /old-items show 301 versus 308, /checkout uses 303 after a POST, and safeNext turns //evil.example and https://evil.example into a redirect to /.

sections.body: After a miss in the request method's tree Gin first tries a trailing-slash redirect, then, if RedirectFixedPath is on, a cleaned case-insensitive redirect. Only then, with HandleMethodNotAllowed on, does it look the path up in every other method's tree. If any match, it sets Allow to those methods, in the order their trees were first created on the engine, and runs the NoMethod chain with status 405; otherwise it runs the NoRoute chain with 404. If your handler writes nothing, Gin falls back to "405 method not allowed" or "404 page not found" as text/plain. Allow lists only methods you registered, so HEAD and OPTIONS never appear by implication. If a load balancer health-checks with HEAD, register it with Match or HEAD; http.Server discards a HEAD response body, but your handler still produces it. CORS preflight OPTIONS requests reach only engine-level middleware, so a CORS middleware must be installed with r.Use to answer them.
sections.title: How Gin chooses between 404, 405 and a redirect

sections.body: NoRoute and NoMethod handlers are combined with engine-level middleware from r.Use only; group middleware never runs for a miss, and c.FullPath() is empty there. Reuse the same error type your handlers return so clients parse every failure the same way, and keep the message fixed rather than echoing the request path, which is attacker-controlled text that may end up in a log viewer or an HTML page. Missing files under StaticFS also run the NoRoute handlers, as the HTML-templates lesson showed. A service that serves both pages and an API can branch on the path prefix.
sections.title: One error shape, including for misses
sections.walkthrough: This fragment assumes the apiError type from the program and a 404.html template loaded with SetHTMLTemplate. Requests under /api/ get the JSON error contract; everything else gets an HTML page with the same 404 status. Only one NoRoute chain exists per engine, so this branch is the single place where that policy lives.

sections.body: 301 and 302 are the historical codes, and clients may change a POST into a GET when following them; browsers also cache a 301 aggressively, so a mistaken permanent redirect is hard to take back. Use 302 or 307 while a move is still tentative. 303 See Other tells the client to fetch the result with GET, the post/redirect/get pattern after a form submission. 307 and 308 preserve the method and the body; 308 is permanent. Gin's own trailing-slash redirects use 301 for GET and 307 for other methods for exactly that reason. c.Redirect panics for codes outside 300 to 308, except 201 Created, and http.Redirect writes its short HTML body only for GET and HEAD. Never redirect to a client-supplied URL without validation: accept only paths that start with a single slash, and reject // and backslashes, because browsers treat /\evil.example like //evil.example, a protocol-relative URL to another host.
sections.title: Pick the redirect status by what must survive

sections.body: Extend the route-table test from the route-groups lesson: for every entry in r.Routes(), send the common methods that are not registered and assert 405, the exact Allow value and a JSON Content-Type. Add HEAD for every GET route you expect monitors to probe, an unknown path, a trailing-slash variant, each redirect's status and Location, and a list of hostile next values including //host, /\host and https://host.
sections.title: Test the misses as carefully as the hits

readings.takeaway: Turn on HandleMethodNotAllowed, answer misses through NoRoute and NoMethod in your normal error format, register HEAD explicitly where it is probed, and use 303, 307 or 308 whenever the method or body must survive a redirect.
readings.title: 404, 405 and redirects in Gin: answer misses in your own format and pick redirect codes by what must survive
wrongAnswers: Yes; Gin runs the GET handler and drops the body
Yes, but only when HandleMethodNotAllowed is enabled

cautions: Routes registered outside the group, or before Use, are public.
Stateless HMAC tokens cannot be revoked before expiry without extra state.
designGuide.cost: One HMAC per request is cheap; the real cost is key management: rotation, storage in a secret manager and a revocation story.
strengths: One verification point covers every route in the group.
Handlers receive a typed principal instead of raw headers.

readings.hint: Would sending the same request again with a freshly issued copy of this token change the outcome?
readings.introduction: Authentication middleware turns an Authorization header into one of two outcomes before any handler runs: a verified principal, or a refusal the client can act on. The bugs live at the edges of that job: a route registered outside the protected group, a MAC compared with ==, a 403 where the client needed a 401, or a debug log that quietly archives every credential it sees.
readings.nuance: 401 means the credentials are missing or invalid, so a retry with good ones may succeed. This token verified, so the refusal is about permission, which RFC 6750 signals with 403 and insufficient_scope.
readings.objective: Write middleware that verifies an HMAC-signed bearer token, stores a typed principal and answers 401 or 403 for the right reasons.
readings.question: A caller sends a valid, unexpired bearer token that lacks the notes:admin scope to an admin-only route. What should the middleware answer?
readings.reviewAnswer: 403 with error="insufficient_scope"

sections.body: Authentication answers who is calling; authorization answers whether that caller may do this. Keep them in separate middleware so each has one reason to refuse. A 401 Unauthorized means the request carried no usable credentials and a retry with valid ones may succeed; RFC 9110 requires a WWW-Authenticate header on every 401 so the client learns which scheme to use. A 403 Forbidden means the server knows exactly who is calling and the answer is still no, so logging in again will not help. RFC 6750 refines this for bearer tokens: a request with no token gets a bare challenge, an invalid or expired token gets error="invalid_token", and a valid token without the needed scope gets 403 with error="insufficient_scope". Neither middleware decides whether note 7 belongs to user-42. That ownership check needs the stored data, so it belongs to the use case, which receives the principal as an argument.
sections.title: Decide what the middleware owns

sections.body: An opaque token is a string the client stores and sends back but never interprets. Here it is base64url(subject|scopes|expiry) followed by a dot and an HMAC-SHA256 tag over those bytes, keyed with a server secret. The verifier recomputes the tag and compares it with hmac.Equal, whose running time does not depend on where the first differing byte is; == on strings or bytes.Equal may stop early and leak how much of a guess was right. Only a payload with a valid tag is parsed, and expiry is checked against an injected clock so tests never sleep. The program forges an admin token by swapping the payload while keeping a real tag, and replays an expired one.
sections.title: Verify the MAC first, then trust the payload
sections.walkthrough: Verify splits at the first dot, decodes both halves and recomputes the tag before parsing anything, so the forged admin payload fails as a bad signature without its scopes ever being read. authenticate compares the scheme with strings.EqualFold because auth schemes are case-insensitive, which is why the lowercase bearer request succeeds. Each refusal sets WWW-Authenticate before AbortWithStatusJSON writes the response, and the rejection log line carries the route and a reason code but no token. c.Set stores the Principal under the unexported principalKey type, and principalFrom is the only reader, so handlers get a typed value instead of re-parsing headers. requireScope runs inside the admin group, after authenticate, and answers 403 with insufficient_scope. The JSON log handler drops the time attribute so the output is stable.
