A shared interfaces package that every package imports

cautions: Pointer DTOs cannot distinguish an omitted field from an explicit null.
A store-level lock does not prevent lost updates between two clients.
designGuide.cost: Two DTOs per resource and an Update callback in the store; worth it as soon as a client sends partial updates.
strengths: Clients can rely on Location, 204 and 409 meaning the same thing everywhere.
Uniqueness is enforced where the data lives, so no check-then-write race.
PATCH can set false and empty values without ambiguity.

readings.hint: Compare what a plain bool holds when the field is missing and when it is false.
readings.introduction: CRUD looks like boilerplate until a client depends on the details: whether create tells it where the new note lives, whether PUT without a body field clears it, whether PATCH with false can unpin a note, and whether a duplicate title is a 400 or a 409. This lesson pins down each answer for the notes resource, on top of a mutex-protected in-memory store behind the Store interface.
readings.nuance: With a plain bool an omitted field and an explicit false both decode to false, so the handler cannot tell "leave it" from "unpin it". A nil pointer marks absence.
readings.objective: Implement create, read, replace, patch and delete for notes with correct status codes, a Location header and presence-aware PATCH fields.
readings.question: A PATCH request sends {"pinned":false}. Why does patchNote use *bool instead of bool for Pinned?
readings.reviewAnswer: nil means absent, so false and "" stay settable
readings.reviewPrompt: Why pointer fields in a PATCH DTO?

sections.body: A resource API is a promise about methods, paths, statuses and headers, and clients code against every part of it. Writing the table first exposes decisions that are easy to fudge in code: who assigns IDs, what a partial update means and which errors exist. Here the server assigns IDs, so POST creates and PUT only replaces an existing note. Titles are unique, which gives the store a real invariant to protect and the API a real reason to answer 409.
sections.code:
POST   /notes        create      201 Created + Location: /notes/{id} + body
                                 400 unreadable body, 409 title already used
GET    /notes/{id}   read        200 + body, 404 unknown id
PUT    /notes/{id}   replace     200 + body, 400 incomplete body, 404, 409
PATCH  /notes/{id}   merge       200 + body, 400 invalid field, 404, 409
DELETE /notes/{id}   remove      204 No Content (empty body), 404 unknown id
sections.title: Write the contract before the handlers
sections.walkthrough: Read each row as a test case. 201 always comes with a Location header pointing at the new resource, so clients never guess URLs. 204 means success with no body: the net/http server rejects a body write for it with http.ErrBodyNotAllowed, and Gin renderers skip the body for that status. 404 and 409 come from domain errors, not from handler logic. 400 is for input the adapter cannot accept; the binding-limits lesson already covers size limits and strict decoding, so this lesson only uses binding tags.

sections.body: The store keeps two maps that must always agree: notes by ID and a unique index from title to ID. Every method takes the mutex, and Update runs a caller-supplied function on a copy while holding the write lock, so read, modify and write happen as one step. Handlers translate HTTP into store calls and use a small writeError helper for now. The program replays a short session against the API and prints each status, Location header and body.
sections.title: Five routes over one locked store
sections.walkthrough: The first POST returns 201 with Location: /notes/n1. The duplicate POST gets 409 from the unique index; it still consumed ID n2 because the handler allocates the ID before inserting, just as a database sequence would, so the next note is n3. PATCH with {"pinned":true} changes one field and keeps the body. PUT with only a title replaces the whole representation, so body becomes "" and pinned becomes false. PATCH with an empty title is rejected with 400 because the field is present and fails min=1. Renaming n3 to an existing title is 409. DELETE answers 204 with no body, and the following GET is 404.

sections.body: putNote has plain fields because PUT sends a complete representation: anything absent takes its zero value, and title is required. patchNote uses pointers because PATCH must tell "not sent" from "set to the zero value"; with a plain bool, {"pinned":false} and {} decode identically. Validator tags cooperate with this: omitempty on a pointer skips only a nil pointer, so a present empty string is still checked against min=1, which is the 400 in the output. One limit remains: JSON null also leaves a pointer nil, so this DTO cannot express "clear this field" the way JSON Merge Patch (RFC 7396) does, where null removes a member. If clients need that, decode into map[string]json.RawMessage or a small optional type that records both presence and null. Whichever you choose, document it and accept application/merge-patch+json if you claim merge-patch semantics.
sections.title: PUT replaces, PATCH merges, pointers carry presence

sections.body: The mutex protects an invariant, not just a map: byID and byTitle change together or not at all. That is why the uniqueness check lives inside Create and Update rather than in a handler that first asks "is this title free?" and then writes; between those two calls another request could take the title. In PostgreSQL the same guarantee comes from a unique index, and the adapter maps SQLSTATE 23505 (unique_violation) to notes.ErrConflict. Get returns a copy of the struct, so callers cannot mutate stored state behind the lock; a Note with slice fields would need a deep copy. The function passed to Update runs under the write lock, so it must be quick and free of I/O. What the lock cannot fix is two clients that each read version one and write back their own edit; that lost update spans two requests and is the subject of the optimistic-concurrency lesson.
sections.title: What the lock protects, and what it cannot

sections.body: Should POST return 200? No: 201 plus Location tells the client a new resource exists and where. Can Location be relative? Yes, RFC 9110 allows a URI reference, resolved against the request URL. Is a second DELETE returning 404 a violation of idempotency? No: idempotency is about the effect on server state, which is the same after one or two deletes; the responses may differ. Should PUT to an unknown ID create it? Only when clients choose IDs; then it returns 201. Is a duplicate title 400 or 409? The request is well formed but conflicts with current state, so 409. Never answer 200 with an error object in the body. Test each row of the contract through ServeHTTP, including the Location header and the empty 204 body.
sections.title: Status-code questions reviewers ask

readings.takeaway: Return 201 with Location on create and 204 with no body on delete, derive 404 and 409 from domain errors, treat PUT as full replacement and give PATCH presence-aware pointer fields.
readings.title: Full CRUD on one resource: exact status codes, a Location header and PUT versus PATCH
wrongAnswers: Pointers make JSON decoding faster for small structs
Gin binding cannot decode JSON into plain bool fields

cautions: Cursors are readable and forgeable; validate them like any input.
No random page access or cheap total count with keyset pagination.
designGuide.cost: A cursor type, a composite index and an allow-list per sortable field; filters and sorts must be designed, not exposed column by column.
strengths: Pages stay correct while rows are inserted or deleted.
Each page costs about the same with a composite index.
Sort input can never become SQL text.

readings.hint: Think about what decides the order of two rows with equal timestamps.
readings.introduction: A GET /notes that returns every row is fine with ten notes and an outage with ten million. Pagination bounds the work per request, but the naive offset version skips or repeats rows when data changes between pages, and a sort parameter pasted into SQL is an injection point. This lesson adds listing, filtering and sorting to the notes API with both failure modes closed.
readings.nuance: Without a unique last sort column the order of ties is unspecified, so a page that ends between them leaves the next query no exact point to resume from.
readings.objective: Serve stable pages of notes with keyset cursors, cap the page size and accept only allow-listed filter and sort parameters.
readings.question: Two notes share the same created_at value. Why must both the cursor and ORDER BY also include the note ID?
readings.reviewAnswer: Ties make page boundaries skip or repeat rows
readings.reviewPrompt: Why add id to every sort order?

sections.body: OFFSET 40 LIMIT 20 asks the database to produce sixty rows and throw away forty, so deep pages get slower as the table grows. Worse, positions are not stable: when a note is inserted at the top between two requests, every row shifts down by one and the next page repeats a note; a delete makes one disappear. Keyset pagination remembers the sort key and ID of the last row returned and asks for rows strictly after that point. With an index on those columns each page costs about the same, and concurrent inserts cannot shift a boundary that is a value rather than a count. The trade-offs are honest ones: no jumping to page 37 and no cheap total count. Offset remains acceptable for small, rarely changing admin tables.
sections.title: Offset pages drift; key-based pages do not

sections.body: parseList is the gate: it rejects malformed query strings and unknown parameters, bounds the limit, checks the sort against the allow-list and decodes the cursor. The store sorts by the chosen key with the ID as tie-breaker, skips everything up to the cursor, and fetches one extra row to learn whether another page exists. The program first shows offset drift on the same data, then walks the cursor pages while a new note arrives, and finally sends invalid queries.
sections.title: List, filter and sort the notes
sections.walkthrough: The offset line returns n5 and n4, then n4 again after n6 is inserted, the classic duplicate. The cursor walk returns n5 n4, then n3 n2, then n1 with more=false; the new n6 does not disturb later pages because it sorts before the cursor and will appear on a fresh first page. n2 and n3 share a timestamp, and the ID breaks the tie deterministically. The decoded cursor is just JSON with the sort, the last key and the last ID. pinned=true with sort=title returns n1 n4, limit=500 is clamped to 100 and echoed back, and the three bad queries each get a 400 naming the problem. The last one matters: URL.Query, and therefore c.Query, silently drops pairs containing a semicolon, while url.ParseQuery reports the error so the API can reject it.

sections.body: If two rows compare equal on the sort key, neither SQL nor slices.SortFunc promises their relative order, and it can differ between two executions of the same query. A page that ends between tied rows then gives the next request no exact place to resume, so a row is skipped or repeated. Appending a unique column, the ID, to every sort order makes the order total, and the cursor must carry both values. Support it with a composite index such as (created_at, id). Watch the key format too. The in-memory model compares keys as strings, so timestamps are formatted at fixed width in UTC. PostgreSQL stores timestamps with microsecond precision while Go keeps nanoseconds, so truncate to microseconds before writing; otherwise the key in the cursor never equals the stored value and the boundary comparison is subtly wrong.
sections.title: A total order needs a tie-breaker

sections.body: Calling the cursor opaque is a contract with clients: they must pass it back unchanged and never build one, so you can change its format later. It is not a security property. base64url is an encoding, and the program decodes the cursor in one line. Treat a cursor like any other input: decode it, validate every field, reject it if it was issued for a different sort, and never place in it anything the caller could not already see. If tampering matters, append an HMAC computed with a server key and verify it before use. Authorization must not depend on the cursor; the owner filter comes from the authenticated request on every page, so a forged cursor can at most move the starting point within the caller's own notes. For the limit, pick a default, clamp at a maximum, echo the effective value and reject zero or non-numeric input with 400.
sections.title: Opaque cursors are encoded, not secret

sections.body: Reject unknown query parameters: a client that types pined=true and silently receives every note has a bug that nobody will notice. For sorting, the allow-list is not just validation; it is the only bridge between user input and SQL text. A placeholder binds a value, never an identifier, so ORDER BY $1 sorts every row by the same constant and no error appears. Interpolating the column name instead is SQL injection. Map each public sort name to a constant clause and build the query from those constants plus placeholders.
sections.title: Allow-lists for filters and sorts, constants for SQL
sections.walkthrough: This fragment is the PostgreSQL side of the same API; run it against a database in your own environment. orderBy and afterCursor are the allow-list expressed as SQL constants, and parseList has already guaranteed that q.sort is one of their keys. Only placeholder numbers are formatted into the string; every client-supplied value, including the cursor key and ID, travels in args. The row comparison (created_at, id) < ($2, $3) matches the ORDER BY direction and can use the composite index. Text keys such as title compare with the column collation in SQL, which may differ from the byte order the in-memory model uses.

readings.takeaway: Page by the last (sort key, id) in a validated opaque cursor, cap the limit, reject unknown parameters, and map allow-listed sort names to constant SQL instead of interpolating them.
readings.title: Paginate with opaque cursors, a bounded limit and a total order; filter only through allow-lists
wrongAnswers: The ID makes the base64 cursor harder to forge
PostgreSQL rejects ORDER BY on a non-unique column

cautions: An unmapped new error kind silently becomes a 500 unless a test checks coverage.
A handler that writes before failing leaves the middleware able only to log.
designGuide.cost: A small taxonomy, one mapping function and a middleware; existing handlers change from writing JSON to returning after c.Error.
strengths: Clients parse one documented error shape and branch on a stable type URI.
Internal error text stays in logs by construction.
Adding a route cannot add a new, undocumented error format.

readings.hint: The domain package does not import net/http.
readings.introduction: By now each notes handler writes its own gin.H{"error": ...}. Clients parse several shapes, someone eventually returns err.Error() and leaks a database host, and nobody can list which statuses an endpoint produces. RFC 9457 supplies a standard envelope. A taxonomy in the domain and one mapping function supply the discipline. The errors-testing lesson established one response owner; this lesson gives that owner a contract.
readings.nuance: One mapping middleware means one table to review, one envelope for clients and no handler that can forget to hide an internal error's text.
readings.objective: Return application/problem+json for every failure by mapping a small domain error taxonomy to HTTP statuses in a single Gin middleware.
readings.question: In the notes API, where should a wrapped notes.ErrConflict become a 409 application/problem+json response?
readings.reviewAnswer: One error middleware, using errors.Is and errors.As
readings.reviewPrompt: Who turns domain errors into HTTP?

sections.body: The notes package defines what can go wrong in business terms: ErrNotFound, ErrConflict and ErrForbidden as sentinel values, and *ValidationError as a type that carries field-level reasons. Services wrap them with fmt.Errorf and %w to add context such as the note ID, and the wrapped chain still matches. The domain does not import net/http and does not know that 404 exists; a CLI or a queue worker can use the same errors. Malformed JSON is different: the domain never sees request bytes, so that error belongs to httpapi. Keep the taxonomy small. Four or five kinds cover most APIs, and each new kind is a decision about how clients should react, not a new spelling of "something failed".
sections.title: Name failures in the domain, not in HTTP

sections.body: Every handler now ends a failure with c.Error(err) and returns; none of them chooses a status. The problems middleware calls c.Next, looks at the last recorded error and asks problemFor, the only mapping table in the service, for a Problem. It logs the cause of server errors, skips writing if a handler already committed a response, and renders application/problem+json. NoRoute records ErrNotFound, so unknown paths get the same envelope.
sections.title: Handlers record, the middleware responds
sections.walkthrough: problemFor checks the typed error first with errors.AsType, the generic counterpart of errors.As in the Go 1.27 standard library, then the sentinels with errors.Is; both see through the %w wrapping, so "load note n9: notes: not found" still maps to 404. The 400 for truncated JSON never repeats the decoder message. The 422 carries the field list from ValidationError, the one error type written for clients. The 500 shows the split: the log line has the full driver message, including user and host, while the body says only Internal Server Error. The last line is an unregistered path, which Gin routes through global middleware and the NoRoute handler, so it is a problem document rather than Gin's plain-text default.

sections.body: RFC 9457, which obsoletes RFC 7807, defines a JSON object served as application/problem+json. type is a URI reference that identifies the problem type and is what clients should branch on; when it is absent it means about:blank, and then title should be the standard phrase for the status code. title is a short summary of the type that should not change between occurrences except for localization. status is advisory and must match the real response status. detail explains this occurrence and should help the client correct the request, not debug the server. instance identifies the occurrence. Extension members such as errors are allowed, and clients must ignore extensions they do not understand.
sections.title: The problem document, member by member
sections.walkthrough: This is the 422 body from the program, pretty-printed. The type URI is a stable identifier under your control and can resolve to human documentation; example.com is a placeholder. title stays the same for every validation failure, while detail and the errors extension describe this request. instance here is the request path; a request ID or a urn:uuid value is also acceptable if support tooling needs to find the matching log line.

sections.body: The text of an arbitrary error is written for developers: it contains SQL fragments, hostnames, user names, file paths and library versions. Public text therefore comes only from the mapping table or from error types designed to be public, such as ValidationError; an unrecognized error becomes a 500 with about:blank and no detail. Log the cause with a request ID and return that ID as an extension member if support needs to correlate. Choose between 403 and 404 deliberately: when the caller may not even know a note exists, answer 404 so the status does not confirm it; use 403 when the caller can see the note but may not perform this action. Two Gin details make the middleware work. Setting Content-Type before c.JSON is preserved, because Gin's JSON renderer only sets the header when it is absent. And when a handler has already written, the middleware must only log, because a second write cannot change a status that is already on the wire.
sections.title: What must never reach the body

sections.body: For each member of the taxonomy and for one unknown error, send a request through ServeHTTP and assert the status, the Content-Type and the decoded body; the API-tests lesson builds this table. Add one test that fails when an exported sentinel has no mapping, so a new error kind cannot silently become a 500. Assert that 500 bodies contain no detail at all, since that is the regression that leaks credentials. Clients should branch on type, so changing a type URI is a breaking change; changing title wording is not.
sections.title: Test the envelope as a contract

readings.takeaway: Let handlers call c.Error with domain errors, map them in one middleware with errors.Is and errors.AsType to application/problem+json, and never copy an unrecognized error's text into the body.
readings.title: One error envelope: RFC 9457 problem details mapped from domain errors in one middleware
wrongAnswers: In each handler, so every route chooses its own status
In the notes service, which returns the HTTP status code

cautions: A separate idempotency store leaves a crash window; prefer one transaction with the effect.
Unscoped keys can replay one tenant's response to another.
designGuide.cost: One record per write request for the retention period, a lease for pending entries and an extra read and write on every POST.
strengths: Clients can retry ambiguous POSTs without creating duplicates.
Changed payloads and concurrent duplicates are rejected explicitly.
Replays return the identical status, headers and body.

readings.hint: The key promises one effect for one request; ask whether this is still the same request.
readings.introduction: A mobile client sends POST /notes, the connection drops before the 201 arrives, and the client retries. Without help the server creates a second note. HTTP defines PUT and DELETE as idempotent; POST is not, so the client supplies a unique key and the server promises that one key yields at most one effect and one stored response. This lesson adds that promise to the notes API.
readings.nuance: Replaying would hand back a note the client did not ask for and hide its bug; running it would allow a second effect. Rejecting with 422 keeps one key bound to one request.
readings.objective: Add Idempotency-Key handling to POST /notes so retries replay the original response, conflicting reuse is rejected and in-flight duplicates wait.
readings.question: A client reuses Idempotency-Key k1 with a different JSON body after the first request succeeded. What should the server do?
readings.reviewAnswer: 422: the key is bound to the first request's fingerprint

sections.body: A timeout is ambiguous: the request may have failed before the handler ran, or succeeded with only the response lost. The client cannot tell, so a safe retry needs the server to remember. The client generates a random key, typically a UUID, for each logical operation and reuses it only when retrying that operation. The server keeps one record per caller and key with a fingerprint of the request, its state and, once finished, the response. Each arrival then has exactly one outcome: a new key runs the handler; a finished identical request is replayed; an identical request still running gets 409; the same key with a different request gets 422; a missing key gets 400. These choices follow the IETF HTTPAPI working group's Idempotency-Key header draft, which is still a draft, so document them in your API contract.
sections.title: Why a retry duplicates, and what the key promises

sections.body: Idempotent runs before the create handler. It reads and restores the body, fingerprints the request, and calls Begin, which checks and reserves the key in one critical section. On a fresh reservation it swaps c.Writer for a captureWriter that copies everything written, runs the handler with c.Next, and stores the status, Location and body. A deferred function releases the reservation when the handler ends in a 5xx or panics. The program holds one request open with channels so the in-progress case is deterministic.
sections.title: A middleware that reserves, captures and replays
sections.walkthrough: The first k1 creates n1. The retry with the same body never reaches the handler: it gets the stored 201, the same Location and Idempotent-Replayed=true. Reusing k1 with a different title is 422, and a request without a key is 400. For k2, a goroutine starts the slow request, and main waits on entered until the handler is inside Create, so the reservation certainly exists; the second k2 then gets 409 with Retry-After. Closing release lets the first k2 finish with 201 for n2. Finally the fake clock moves 25 hours forward, past the 24-hour retention, and the old k1 creates n3: an expired key is a new request. Three notes exist, not five.

sections.body: The fingerprint is SHA-256 over the method, the route pattern from c.FullPath and the raw body bytes. Byte equality is strict: a client that re-serializes the same JSON with different key order or spacing gets 422. Most APIs accept that and tell clients to resend the identical bytes; canonicalizing JSON before hashing is possible but easy to get subtly wrong. Scope every key by the authenticated principal. Without scope, two tenants that happen to choose the same key would see each other's responses, a data leak rather than a duplicate. Bound the key length and the body size before reading; the binding-limits lesson covers MaxBytesReader. Store whatever the client needs to treat a replay as the original, here status, Location and body. The Idempotent-Replayed header is a convention some APIs use, not a standard, but it makes replays visible in logs and client debugging.
sections.title: Fingerprints, scope and what gets stored

sections.body: Begin must check and reserve atomically or two concurrent first attempts both run. The mutex does it here; in PostgreSQL use INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING and check the affected row count, and in Redis use SET with NX and an expiry. A pending record also needs a lease: if the process dies mid-request, nothing releases it, and every retry gets 409 until the record expires. Give pending records a short lock expiry separate from the retention TTL, and make the retention longer than any client's retry window. The deeper gap is that the note and the idempotency record live in different stores. A crash after the note is committed but before Finish loses the stored response, and a retry after the lease runs out creates a duplicate; releasing on a 5xx has the same hole if the effect committed before the error. The robust design writes the idempotency record in the same database transaction as the note, so the effect and the response commit together.
sections.title: In progress, expiry and the crash window

sections.body: Cover each branch through ServeHTTP: a fresh key, an identical replay that leaves exactly one note in the store, a changed body that returns 422, a missing key, an in-progress duplicate held open with channels as the program does, expiry driven by an injected clock and a 5xx that releases the key so the retry runs again. Add a test that fires many identical requests from goroutines and asserts that the handler ran once, and run the suite with -race. Assert the replayed body byte for byte, because the promise is the same response, not a similar one.
sections.title: Test every outcome, including the concurrent one

readings.takeaway: Reserve each principal-scoped key atomically with a request fingerprint, replay the stored response for identical retries, answer 422 for a changed payload and 409 while in progress, and retain records longer than clients retry.
readings.title: Make POST safe to retry with Idempotency-Key: fingerprint, reserve, replay and expire
wrongAnswers: Replay the first response, because the key matches
Run the new request and overwrite the stored response

cautions: A check in the handler followed by an unconditional write still races.
Weak ETags never satisfy If-Match, so writes need strong validators.
designGuide.cost: A version column, a conditional UPDATE and client code that handles 412 by re-reading and merging.
strengths: Concurrent edits are detected instead of silently overwritten.
No locks are held while clients read or think.
Uses standard HTTP headers and statuses that clients and proxies understand.

readings.hint: One status means a condition was evaluated and failed; another means no condition was sent.
readings.introduction: Two people open the same note. One adds a line; the other fixes the title from the copy loaded earlier, and that second save quietly erases the first edit. Each request was valid on its own. The bug is that the server never asked which version the client was editing. HTTP already has the vocabulary for that question: ETag, If-Match, 412 Precondition Failed and 428 Precondition Required.
readings.nuance: 412 reports a precondition that was present and false. RFC 6585 defines 428 for a server that requires a precondition the request did not include.
readings.objective: Version the notes resource, expose the version as an ETag and require If-Match on writes so a stale client cannot overwrite a newer edit.
readings.question: The notes API requires conditional writes. A client sends PUT /notes/n1 without an If-Match header. Which response is correct?
readings.reviewAnswer: 428 Precondition Required

sections.body: The store's mutex from the CRUD lesson makes each write atomic, but the dangerous gap is not inside a request. It is between one client's GET and its later PUT, while another client writes. A lock cannot cover that gap without holding it across user think time, and abandoned locks are worse than the original bug. Optimistic concurrency accepts that conflicts are rare and detects them at write time instead: every note carries a version, every successful write increments it, and a write names the version it was based on. If the stored version has moved, the write is refused and the client decides what to do. Nothing is locked while people read.
sections.title: A lost update spans two requests

sections.body: GET returns the version as a strong ETag such as "1". The guarded PUT requires If-Match, compares it with the current version and asks the store to replace the note only if the version is still the one it checked. The naive route with no checks runs first to reproduce the bug, then the guarded route replays the same two edits.
sections.title: ETag out, If-Match in, compare-and-swap in the store
sections.walkthrough: On the naive route both writes succeed and the final body is "flights": client A's hotel is gone and nobody was told. On the guarded route both clients read ETag "1". A writes with If-Match "1" and gets 200 with ETag "2". B writes from the stale copy with If-Match "1" and gets 412. Without If-Match B gets 428, so skipping the header is not a way around the check. W/"2" names the current version but is weak, and If-Match uses strong comparison, so it fails too. B re-reads, gets "2", reapplies the title change onto the current body and receives ETag "3"; the final note keeps both edits. Replace re-checks the version under its own lock because another writer can win between the handler's Get and the write.

sections.body: RFC 9110 defines an entity tag as a quoted string, optionally prefixed with W/ to mark it weak. If-Match is evaluated with strong comparison, so a weak tag can never satisfy it, and the asterisk matches any current representation, which is useful to say "update only if it exists". When the condition is false the server must not perform the method; the usual answer is 412, and RFC 9110 also permits a 2xx when the server can verify that the requested change is already reflected in the current state. RFC 6585 adds 428 for a server that requires conditional requests and receives one without a condition. Send the new ETag with every successful write so the client does not need an extra GET. PATCH needs exactly the same guard as PUT: a partial update made from stale assumptions is still a lost update. In the full service, 412 and 428 go through the problems middleware as two more problem types.
sections.title: The rules HTTP already defines

sections.body: The version check and the increment must be one operation in the store. A handler that reads the version, compares it and then issues an unconditional write has a race between the compare and the write. In SQL the condition goes into the UPDATE itself, and a statement that matched no rows tells you the condition failed. Do not use updated_at as the version: clock resolution and skew make two writes look simultaneous. Increment the version on every change that alters the representation, and if the representation includes data from elsewhere, such as an author name from another table, either include that in the version or derive the ETag from a hash of the representation.
sections.title: Make the check atomic where the data lives
sections.walkthrough: This fragment is the PostgreSQL adapter for the same Replace contract; run it against your own database. The WHERE clause checks ID, owner and version in the same statement that increments the version, so two writers holding version 5 cannot both succeed; the second matches zero rows. RETURNING gives the new version for the ETag. On sql.ErrNoRows a second query distinguishes a deleted note, which maps to 404, from a version that moved on, which maps to 412.

sections.body: On 412 a client re-reads, merges or shows the conflict to the person, and retries with the fresh ETag. Automatically resending the same body with the new ETag is just last-write-wins with extra steps. Conditional writes also interact with retries: if a PUT succeeded but the response was lost, the retry with the old If-Match gets 412 from this implementation, and the client should re-read and notice its change is already there. Test the contract through ServeHTTP: missing header is 428, a stale tag is 412, a weak tag is 412, a fresh tag is 200 with the next ETag, and two goroutines writing with the same tag produce exactly one 200.
sections.title: What clients and tests must do

readings.takeaway: Expose a version as a strong ETag, require If-Match on PUT and PATCH with 428 when it is absent, and let the store compare and increment the version atomically, answering 412 on mismatch.
readings.title: Stop lost updates with versions, ETag and If-Match: 428 when missing, 412 when stale
wrongAnswers: 412 Precondition Failed, because no version matched
200 OK, applying the write as last-write-wins

cautions: float64 decoding loses precision for integers above 2^53.
Fakes do not prove the real store works; keep separate integration tests.
designGuide.cost: A fake per dependency, a test helper and the discipline to inject time and IDs everywhere.
strengths: Tests the real middleware chain and error mapping in milliseconds.
Whole-body comparison catches leaks and accidental fields.
New cases are one table row, so regressions get reproduced cheaply.

readings.hint: Consider what changes in the bytes when the same object is encoded twice.
readings.introduction: Tests that call a handler function directly miss the bugs that live between handlers: middleware order, error mapping, headers and the exact JSON a client parses. Sending requests through the router production uses, with a fake store behind it, tests the API contract in milliseconds. A table turns the next case into a few lines, and asserting whole bodies is what catches the regression that a status check waves through.
readings.nuance: Two encodings of one object can differ in key order and spacing. Decoding compares values, and because DeepEqual still sees every member, an unexpected detail field fails the test.
readings.objective: Write table-driven tests that send requests through the real Gin router with fakes and assert status, contract headers and semantically compared JSON bodies.
readings.question: Why does assertJSONEqual decode both the expected and the actual body into any before comparing them?
readings.reviewAnswer: Key order and whitespace are not part of the contract

sections.body: In these tests everything a request touches in production is real except the outermost dependencies. The engine, the problems middleware, the handlers and the notes service are the production code, built through the same constructors main uses. The store, the clock and the ID source are fakes injected as the dependencies lesson showed, which makes every body deterministic. Each case builds its own fake and router, so cases share nothing and can run in parallel. Assert three things per response: the status, every header that is part of the contract such as Location, Content-Type, ETag or Retry-After, and the entire body as a JSON value. A storage adapter gets its own integration tests against a real database; mixing the two makes API tests slow and flaky.
sections.title: Test the router, fake only the edges

sections.body: The test file lives next to the handlers but uses the external package httpapi_test, so it can only call what main can call: NewRouter, NewHandler and the notes constructors. That keeps the tests honest about the public wiring. TestMain sets Gin's mode once, because SetMode writes a process-wide variable and parallel subtests must not race on it.
sections.title: handler_test.go: the table and the assertions
sections.walkthrough: This fragment belongs in internal/httpapi of the module from the layout lesson and runs there with go test -race ./internal/httpapi. Each table row names the request and the expected contract. t.Run gives every case its own name in the output, and t.Parallel is safe because the router and fake are per case; since Go 1.22 the loop variable tc is a fresh variable on each iteration, so the closure needs no copy. newTestRouter uses t.Helper and t.Fatal for wiring errors. assertJSONEqual decodes both sides into any and compares them with reflect.DeepEqual, reporting the full actual body on mismatch. fakeStore, with a mutex and an err field, lives in fake_test.go in the same package.

sections.body: The runnable model condenses the notes and httpapi packages into one file and runs the same four cases three times: against the current build, against a regressed build with status-only checks, and against the regressed build with full checks. The regression is a plausible "debugging aid": the problems middleware copies err.Error() into detail for unexpected errors.
sections.title: The same table, runnable, against a regression
sections.walkthrough: check sends one request and collects failures instead of calling t.Errorf, so main can print a PASS or FAIL line per case. Header names are checked in sorted order to keep output stable. The current build passes everything; note that the expected create body lists keys in a different order and with spaces, and still matches. On the regressed build, status-only checks pass all four cases, because a leaking 500 is still a 500. Full checks fail the store-failure case and print the body that would have reached clients, with the database address in detail.

sections.body: Byte comparison breaks for reasons that are not part of the contract: key order in maps, field order after a struct refactor, whitespace, and HTML escaping, since encoding/json escapes <, > and & by default and Gin's c.PureJSON does not. Decoding both sides into any and comparing with reflect.DeepEqual compares values instead. It is still strict in the useful direction: an extra member, a missing member and a null where a string was expected all fail, which is exactly how the leaked detail was caught. Two caveats remain. Numbers decode to float64, so integers above 2^53 lose precision; decode with json.Decoder.UseNumber when IDs or amounts are large. And volatile fields should be made deterministic by injecting the clock and ID source rather than deleted before comparing, because deleted fields are untested fields.
sections.title: Compare JSON by meaning, and know the limits

sections.body: For each route, include the success path with its headers, every error kind the problems middleware maps and one failing store that must produce a bare 500. Add middleware-level rows: an unknown route, an oversized body, a missing Idempotency-Key, a missing or stale If-Match. Where a request has side effects, inspect the fake afterwards; a replayed idempotent POST must leave exactly one note. Run with -race and -count=1, and occasionally with -shuffle=on to surface hidden ordering between cases. When a bug escapes, its reproduction becomes a new row before the fix.
sections.title: What the table should cover

readings.takeaway: Drive tests through the production router with fakes for the store, clock and IDs, and assert status, contract headers and the whole JSON body compared semantically, so a leaked detail fails the build.
readings.title: Table-driven API tests through the real router: status, headers and JSON compared by meaning
wrongAnswers: httptest cannot expose the body until it is decoded
It ignores extra members, so tests survive new fields

cautions: URL.Redacted masks only the password; tokens in query strings still leak.
Using the signal context as BaseContext cancels draining requests.
designGuide.cost: A config package with a test table and a slightly longer main; both are cheaper than one misconfigured production start.
strengths: Bad deployments fail before serving, with every problem listed.
All wiring is in one short function that names every dependency.
Shutdown has one owner and one budget taken from configuration.

readings.hint: Follow the signal context down to each request's r.Context().
readings.introduction: The last piece of the notes API is the code that runs first. A typo in an environment variable should stop a deploy with a clear message, not start a server with a default timeout, a debug-mode router or a proxy list that trusts the whole internet. This lesson builds the configuration loader, then assembles every package from the earlier lessons in cmd/api/main.go.
readings.nuance: Every request context derives from BaseContext, so cancelling it on SIGTERM aborts the in-flight requests that a graceful Shutdown is meant to let finish.
readings.objective: Load and validate configuration from the environment, fail fast with every problem listed, and wire store, service, handlers, engine and http.Server with signal-driven shutdown.
readings.question: Why should run not set http.Server.BaseContext to return the signal.NotifyContext context?
readings.reviewAnswer: No: SIGTERM would cancel requests that are draining

sections.body: Environment variables are untyped strings set by people and deployment templates, so they fail in predictable ways. A duration written as 5 without a unit does not parse. A misspelled name is silently ignored and the default applies. A value can parse correctly and still be dangerous, such as a shutdown budget longer than the platform waits before killing the process, or a trusted-proxy range of 0.0.0.0/0. And a database URL printed at startup leaks its password into logs. The loader answers each one: typed fields, explicit ranges, an error for unknown names under the application prefix, defaults that are safe in production, and a String method that redacts secrets. It also collects every problem before returning, so one failed deploy shows the whole list instead of one error per attempt.
sections.title: Configuration is input: parse it, bound it, reject it

sections.body: Load takes the environment as a slice of KEY=value strings, the shape os.Environ returns, rather than calling os.Getenv itself. That keeps it a pure function: tests pass literal slices, and main passes the real environment. Small closures parse each kind of value and append to a shared error list, cross-field rules run at the end, and errors.Join combines everything into one error whose message has one line per problem.
sections.title: Load, validate and print the effective settings
sections.walkthrough: The first configuration is valid: the database URL prints with its password replaced by xxxxx, because URL.Redacted masks only the password component, and the single proxy address becomes a /32 prefix. HOME is ignored because only the NOTES_ prefix is checked. With no variables at all the defaults are complete and conservative: release mode, bounded timeouts and no trusted proxies; the memory store default suits development, and a production deploy sets NOTES_STORE=postgres. The bad configuration reports six problems at once: a misspelled name, a duration without a unit, a shutdown budget above the 25-second ceiling, an address without a colon, a proxy range that would trust every client and a missing database URL that the postgres store requires.

sections.body: main does nothing but call run and translate its error into an exit status. run loads configuration, creates the signal context, builds the graph from the inside out, binds the listener, serves, and on a signal drains with a budget. Every constructor from the earlier lessons appears exactly once here, and no other package names a concrete type from another package.
sections.title: The composition root
sections.walkthrough: Run this fragment in your own environment; it opens a real socket. Because run returns errors instead of exiting, its deferred calls always execute before os.Exit. gin.SetMode runs before NewRouter calls gin.New, and NewRouter returns the error from SetTrustedProxies, so a bad list stops startup. net.Listen binds before the serving goroutine starts, so a busy port is an immediate error rather than a log line from a goroutine. On SIGTERM the context is cancelled and context.Cause reports "terminated signal received". stop restores default signal handling, Shutdown drains within cfg.ShutdownTimeout using a fresh context, Close drops whatever remains if the budget runs out, and ErrServerClosed from Serve is the normal result.

sections.body: Do not pass the signal context to http.Server.BaseContext. Every request context derives from it, so the first SIGTERM would cancel the very requests Shutdown is trying to let finish. Gin reads GIN_MODE once, in its package init, and the fragment then overrides it with SetMode; pick one source of truth, here the validated config, so two settings cannot disagree. The 25-second ceiling on the shutdown budget exists to fit under a platform grace period such as the Kubernetes default of 30 seconds, leaving time for the remaining teardown. Readiness withdrawal, header and idle timeouts, and joining background workers are covered in the server-lifecycle lesson; this root only has to give them one owner and one budget. If a Postgres adapter replaces the memory store, open it before the listener and close it after Shutdown returns, so no request runs against a closed pool.
sections.title: Startup and shutdown details that bite

sections.body: Load is a pure function of a slice, so a table test covers every rule: each default, each range edge, each unknown name, the redacted String output and the combined error text. The composition root is harder to unit test, which is why it should stay thin. A useful refactor is run(ctx, environ) with the signal context created in main: an integration test can then start the service on 127.0.0.1:0, send one request, cancel the context and assert a clean return within the budget, without sending real signals. Log the effective configuration once at startup; when an incident starts with "which timeout was this pod running with?", that line answers it.
sections.title: Test startup like any other code

readings.takeaway: Parse configuration into a typed, bounded struct that reports every error at once and redacts secrets, then wire store, service, handlers, engine and server in main, with signal.NotifyContext starting a budgeted Shutdown.
readings.title: Start from validated configuration and wire the whole service in one composition root
wrongAnswers: Shutdown would then wait forever for that context
BaseContext applies only to HTTP/2 connections

lessons.explanation: Gin is a router, a request context and a middleware chain built on top of net/http. A *gin.Engine is an ordinary http.Handler, so everything you know about http.Server, httptest and timeouts still applies. Start with a function that returns a configured engine: main can serve it, and a test can call it directly.
lessons.objective: Build a Gin engine, register routes with a path parameter and exercise them without opening a port.
lessons.title: Your first Gin service: an engine, two routes and a test request

lessons.explanation: Every Gin route is a template stored in a radix tree. The router decides which handler runs, what c.Param returns and whether the client gets a redirect instead of your handler. Most routing bugs are not in handler code: they are a trailing slash, an encoded slash or two templates that cannot share a prefix. Learn the matching rules once and those bugs become predictable.
lessons.objective: Declare Gin route templates with :param and *wildcard, predict how slashes and escapes resolve, and label metrics with c.FullPath().
lessons.title: Path parameters in Gin: :param takes one segment, *wildcard takes the rest, conflicts panic at boot

lessons.explanation: Every query or form value reaches your handler as a string that may be missing, empty, repeated or malformed. Gin offers several helpers that look interchangeable but answer different questions. Choosing the wrong one turns limit=abc into limit 0, or a deliberately empty field into a default the client never asked for.
lessons.objective: Read query and form values with the Gin helper that matches the case, convert them with strconv and reject bad input with a clear 400.
lessons.title: Query strings and forms in Gin: tell absent from empty, parse numbers strictly, bound every limit

lessons.explanation: r.Group("/api/v1") looks like a folder that routes live in, with middleware guarding the door. It is really a registration helper: when you add a route, Gin copies the group's prefix and handler list into that route, and the group plays no part when requests arrive. That one fact explains the most common group bug and tells you how to test for it.
lessons.objective: Organize a Gin API into nested, versioned groups with scoped middleware and prove with r.Routes() that every route has the protection you intended.
lessons.title: Gin route groups: prefixes and middleware are copied at registration, so test the route table

lessons.explanation: The bytes a handler writes are a public contract: field names, which fields exist, how characters are escaped, the Content-Type and the status. Gin has five JSON renderers that look interchangeable and are not, and c.JSON will happily publish every field of whatever struct you hand it, including the ones you add next year.
lessons.objective: Choose between c.JSON, PureJSON, IndentedJSON, SecureJSON and AsciiJSON by their exact output, set status codes deliberately and render a response DTO with correct omitempty and omitzero tags.
lessons.title: Gin JSON responses: know what each renderer writes and return a DTO, never your storage model

lessons.explanation: A single request carries input in four places: path parameters, the query string, headers and the body. Gin has a binder and a struct tag for each, and they compose well as long as you respect two rules the API does not advertise. Every binder validates the entire struct it fills, and a request body can be read only once unless you ask Gin to keep a copy.
lessons.objective: Bind each request source with its own Gin binder and tag, predict what content-type-driven ShouldBind reads, and decode one body twice with ShouldBindBodyWithJSON.
lessons.title: Gin binding sources: bind path, query, headers and body separately, and cache the body to read it twice

lessons.explanation: Gin's binding tags cover shape: required, lengths, ranges, enumerations. Real input also has domain rules, such as a SKU format or an address that is required unless the customer picks the order up. Gin's validator accepts both kinds, but the default error text names Go structs and fields, which makes a poor API. This lesson adds the rules and a response format you can keep stable.
lessons.objective: Register a custom tag and a struct-level rule on Gin's validator, validate slice elements with dive and convert validator errors into a stable field-level JSON response.
lessons.title: Custom validators in Gin: register domain rules once and return field errors clients can rely on

lessons.explanation: Gin middleware is an ordinary handler that happens to run before others in the same chain. Most middleware bugs come from a wrong mental model of that chain: expecting Abort to return, expecting a middleware without c.Next to stop the request, or reading a status before the handler has chosen it. This lesson builds four realistic middleware functions and traces exactly what runs.
lessons.objective: Write Gin middleware that runs code after c.Next, stops the chain with Abort and return, shares typed values through c.Set and c.Get, and is ordered so logs see the final outcome.
lessons.title: Writing Gin middleware: what c.Next returns to, what Abort does not do, and typed request values

lessons.explanation: An upload is attacker-controlled bytes wrapped in attacker-controlled labels. The filename, the declared Content-Type and the size all come from the client, and so does the number of parts. c.FormFile makes accepting a file one line long, which is exactly why the limits, the type decision and the storage name have to be written deliberately around it.
lessons.objective: Accept a multipart upload in Gin with a hard size cap, decide its type from its content, generate the storage name yourself and test it with a request built by mime/multipart.
lessons.title: File uploads in Gin: cap the request, sniff the bytes and never let the client name the file

lessons.explanation: Gin can render server-side HTML with very little code, and Go's html/template does the hardest part, escaping, for you. What Gin leaves to you are the operational decisions: how templates reach the binary, what happens when a template fails halfway, whether a directory listing is exposed and how long browsers and CDNs may keep each file.
lessons.objective: Render html/template pages with c.HTML from templates parsed out of an embedded file system, serve embedded static assets with StaticFS and set cache headers per kind of asset.
lessons.title: Server-rendered HTML in Gin: embed the templates, trust contextual escaping, cache assets on purpose

lessons.explanation: A Gin engine answers misses on its own: a plain-text 404 for unknown paths and, by default, the same 404 for a known path with the wrong method. API clients that expect JSON errors choke on the text, and a 404 for a wrong method sends whoever is debugging in the wrong direction. A few lines of configuration fix both, and the same lesson applies to redirects: the status code decides whether the method and body survive.
lessons.objective: Configure NoRoute, NoMethod and HandleMethodNotAllowed for consistent JSON 404 and 405 responses with a correct Allow header, and choose between 301, 302, 303, 307 and 308 for redirects.
lessons.title: 404, 405 and redirects in Gin: answer misses in your own format and pick redirect codes by what must survive

units.title: Gin foundations
units.translationNote: Every example runs against upstream Gin v1.12 through httptest in your native development environment. The app's teaching adapter does not promise every Gin API or network-server capability.

lessons.explanation: A Gin engine is an HTTP adapter with a middleware chain. Group prefixes and registration order decide which handlers participate; the framework does not supply your business transaction. Follow one request before introducing authentication, metrics or error middleware. In particular, Abort stops pending handlers but does not return from the current Go function.
lessons.objective: Explain route groups, middleware order and the difference between Abort and return.
lessons.title: Gin routing and middleware: follow the chain and stop it deliberately

lessons.explanation: Binding converts a request into a Go value. It does not prove authorization or a business invariant, and it does not by itself impose your desired body-size budget. A robust handler limits input first, chooses whether errors are returned or immediately written, validates normalized values and only then calls the use case. Return one deliberate response instead of letting several layers compete to write it.
lessons.objective: Reject oversized or invalid input before performing a business side effect.
lessons.title: Gin input: size limits, binding and business validation are separate

lessons.explanation: Gin reuses contexts after a handler returns. Passing the original *gin.Context into a goroutine can observe another request’s mutable state. Copy is useful for limited read-only context access, but it does not extend the response writer’s lifetime, clone every referenced object or give detached work a durable owner. Prefer extracting immutable job input and handing it to a deliberately managed queue.
lessons.objective: Give background work a bounded owner without keeping a pooled Gin context alive.
lessons.title: Gin contexts and goroutines: extract a job, do not retain the response

lessons.explanation: A reverse proxy may supply the original client address, but a direct client can also send X-Forwarded-For. If a Go service trusts forwarding headers from every peer, address-based controls can be bypassed. Configure exactly which proxy origins are trusted and make the edge replace or sanitize incoming forwarding headers. An IP address remains a network observation, not a user credential.
lessons.objective: Configure proxy trust explicitly and keep client IP separate from authentication.
lessons.title: Trusted proxies: forwarded headers are not proof of identity

lessons.explanation: Framework recovery can keep a panic from crashing a request-serving goroutine, but it cannot undo a committed database write or decide whether a remote operation succeeded. Expected application errors should travel through a deliberate mapping policy. Assign one layer to produce the response, and test both its status and public body rather than checking only that the handler returned.
lessons.objective: Test handler contracts through ServeHTTP without confusing recovery with rollback.
lessons.title: Gin errors and tests: one response owner, explicit failure cases

lessons.explanation: A router handles requests, while net/http.Server owns listener behavior and connection budgets. A short r.Run example is useful for a tutorial, but a deployed service needs an explicit startup and shutdown owner. Readiness, request admission, long-lived streams, background workers and shared clients must fit the same lifecycle rather than each inventing its own stop signal.
lessons.objective: Configure native server timeouts and distinguish HTTP drain from worker completion.
lessons.title: Gin in production: the http.Server owns budgets and shutdown

lessons.explanation: Authentication middleware turns an Authorization header into one of two outcomes before any handler runs: a verified principal, or a refusal the client can act on. The bugs live at the edges of that job: a route registered outside the protected group, a MAC compared with ==, a 403 where the client needed a 401, or a debug log that quietly archives every credential it sees.
lessons.objective: Write middleware that verifies an HMAC-signed bearer token, stores a typed principal and answers 401 or 403 for the right reasons.
lessons.title: Bearer authentication in Gin: verify once at the group boundary, hand handlers a typed principal

lessons.explanation: CORS is the protocol a server uses to tell a browser which other origins may read its responses. It relaxes the same-origin policy; it never tightens it. Done carelessly it either breaks a legitimate front end or lets any website read a signed-in user's data. Done correctly it is still not authentication, authorization or CSRF protection, and the server has to keep enforcing those on its own.
lessons.objective: Implement CORS middleware that answers preflights, echoes only allow-listed origins, sets Vary correctly and is never mistaken for access control.
lessons.title: CORS by hand in Gin: an exact origin allow-list, real preflights and Vary: Origin

lessons.explanation: A rate limiter protects shared capacity from one noisy client. Three decisions matter more than the algorithm: what identifies a client, how much memory the limiter may use, and what a refused client is told. Choose the key badly and an attacker gets a fresh bucket on every request. Forget the memory bound and the limiter becomes the leak it was meant to prevent.
lessons.objective: Limit each client with golang.org/x/time/rate, pick a key clients cannot forge, bound the limiter map and refuse with 429 and Retry-After.
lessons.title: Rate limiting in Gin: a token bucket per identity, a bounded map and an honest Retry-After

lessons.explanation: An access log is what you search during an incident. It is only useful if every line carries the same small set of fields, if one request can be followed across services by an ID, and if the log never becomes a second copy of your users' credentials. Gin's built-in Logger prints raw paths with query strings as text, so production services usually replace it with middleware built on log/slog.
lessons.objective: Add request-ID middleware and a structured slog access log that records low-cardinality routes, redacts credentials and can be tested byte for byte.
lessons.title: Request IDs and access logs in Gin: log the route template and the ID, never the credential

lessons.explanation: A request stuck on a slow dependency holds a goroutine, a connection and often a database slot. A deadline bounds that wait, but only if every call below the handler receives the context that carries it. Deadlines are cooperative: Go cannot stop a goroutine from outside, so the safe design lets the handler notice expiry and write the response itself instead of racing it from another goroutine.
lessons.objective: Give each request a deadline that downstream calls inherit, map its expiry to 504, and avoid the timeout patterns that race on the response.
lessons.title: Request deadlines in Gin: one context budget, cooperative handlers, no writes from a second goroutine

lessons.explanation: Server-Sent Events keep one HTTP response open and append small text events to it; the browser's EventSource parses them and reconnects on its own. The protocol is simple, and the engineering is all in the lifecycle. Every event must be flushed through buffers, idle streams need heartbeats, the handler must notice when the client leaves, and the server's write deadline must not cut the stream short.
lessons.objective: Stream SSE from a Gin handler that flushes events, sends heartbeats, ends when the client leaves and survives http.Server's WriteTimeout.
lessons.title: Server-Sent Events in Gin: flush every event, send heartbeats, stop on the request context

lessons.explanation: Health endpoints and request counters are how the platform and the on-call engineer see a service from outside. Each answers a narrow question: should this process be restarted, should it receive traffic right now, and how is each route behaving. Mixing up the first two causes restart storms. Labeling counters with raw paths makes the metrics system the next thing to fall over.
lessons.objective: Separate liveness from readiness, check dependencies within a short budget, and count requests by route template and status class.
lessons.title: Health and metrics in Gin: simple liveness, budgeted readiness, counters keyed by route template

lessons.explanation: A conditional GET lets a client that already holds a copy ask whether it is still current. When it is, the server answers 304 Not Modified with no body, which saves bandwidth and the client's parsing time. The mechanism has three parts: a validator on every response, a comparison on every request, and a Cache-Control policy that decides who may keep a copy. The policy is where private data leaks.
lessons.objective: Serve ETag and Last-Modified validators, answer conditional requests with 304, and choose Cache-Control so private data never lands in a shared cache.
lessons.title: Conditional GETs in Gin: strong ETags from response bytes, 304 Not Modified and safe Cache-Control

units.summary: Middleware, bounded input, authentication, CORS, rate limits, logging, timeouts, streaming, health, caching and shutdown.
units.title: Gin in production
units.translationNote: Worked upstream Gin examples for your native development environment. The app's teaching adapter does not promise every Gin API or network-server capability.

lessons.explanation: One main.go holding handlers, SQL and business rules works until the first test, the second developer or the second storage backend. This unit grows a single notes API over nine lessons, so this first lesson fixes where each piece lives. Later lessons then add CRUD, pagination, problem details, idempotency and versioning without moving code between packages.
lessons.objective: Organize a Gin API into cmd/api, httpapi, notes and store packages whose imports point toward the domain, with all concrete wiring in main.
lessons.title: Lay out a Gin service so every import points toward the domain

lessons.explanation: A handler that reaches for a package-level database variable works on the first day and fights you afterwards: tests share state, parallel tests race, and no signature tells a reviewer what the handler can touch. Passing dependencies through a constructor makes them visible, replaceable and checked by the compiler. This lesson does that for the notes API, including the clock and the ID source.
lessons.objective: Write handlers as methods on a struct built by a constructor, depend on small consumer-defined interfaces and swap in a fake store for tests.
lessons.title: Give Gin handlers their dependencies through a struct, not globals or context keys

lessons.explanation: CRUD looks like boilerplate until a client depends on the details: whether create tells it where the new note lives, whether PUT without a body field clears it, whether PATCH with false can unpin a note, and whether a duplicate title is a 400 or a 409. This lesson pins down each answer for the notes resource, on top of a mutex-protected in-memory store behind the Store interface.
lessons.objective: Implement create, read, replace, patch and delete for notes with correct status codes, a Location header and presence-aware PATCH fields.
lessons.title: Full CRUD on one resource: exact status codes, a Location header and PUT versus PATCH

lessons.explanation: A GET /notes that returns every row is fine with ten notes and an outage with ten million. Pagination bounds the work per request, but the naive offset version skips or repeats rows when data changes between pages, and a sort parameter pasted into SQL is an injection point. This lesson adds listing, filtering and sorting to the notes API with both failure modes closed.
lessons.objective: Serve stable pages of notes with keyset cursors, cap the page size and accept only allow-listed filter and sort parameters.
lessons.title: Paginate with opaque cursors, a bounded limit and a total order; filter only through allow-lists

lessons.explanation: By now each notes handler writes its own gin.H{"error": ...}. Clients parse several shapes, someone eventually returns err.Error() and leaks a database host, and nobody can list which statuses an endpoint produces. RFC 9457 supplies a standard envelope. A taxonomy in the domain and one mapping function supply the discipline. The errors-testing lesson established one response owner; this lesson gives that owner a contract.
lessons.objective: Return application/problem+json for every failure by mapping a small domain error taxonomy to HTTP statuses in a single Gin middleware.
lessons.title: One error envelope: RFC 9457 problem details mapped from domain errors in one middleware

lessons.explanation: A mobile client sends POST /notes, the connection drops before the 201 arrives, and the client retries. Without help the server creates a second note. HTTP defines PUT and DELETE as idempotent; POST is not, so the client supplies a unique key and the server promises that one key yields at most one effect and one stored response. This lesson adds that promise to the notes API.
lessons.objective: Add Idempotency-Key handling to POST /notes so retries replay the original response, conflicting reuse is rejected and in-flight duplicates wait.
lessons.title: Make POST safe to retry with Idempotency-Key: fingerprint, reserve, replay and expire

lessons.explanation: Two people open the same note. One adds a line; the other fixes the title from the copy loaded earlier, and that second save quietly erases the first edit. Each request was valid on its own. The bug is that the server never asked which version the client was editing. HTTP already has the vocabulary for that question: ETag, If-Match, 412 Precondition Failed and 428 Precondition Required.
lessons.objective: Version the notes resource, expose the version as an ETag and require If-Match on writes so a stale client cannot overwrite a newer edit.
lessons.title: Stop lost updates with versions, ETag and If-Match: 428 when missing, 412 when stale

lessons.explanation: Tests that call a handler function directly miss the bugs that live between handlers: middleware order, error mapping, headers and the exact JSON a client parses. Sending requests through the router production uses, with a fake store behind it, tests the API contract in milliseconds. A table turns the next case into a few lines, and asserting whole bodies is what catches the regression that a status check waves through.
lessons.objective: Write table-driven tests that send requests through the real Gin router with fakes and assert status, contract headers and semantically compared JSON bodies.
lessons.title: Table-driven API tests through the real router: status, headers and JSON compared by meaning

lessons.explanation: The last piece of the notes API is the code that runs first. A typo in an environment variable should stop a deploy with a clear message, not start a server with a default timeout, a debug-mode router or a proxy list that trusts the whole internet. This lesson builds the configuration loader, then assembles every package from the earlier lessons in cmd/api/main.go.
lessons.objective: Load and validate configuration from the environment, fail fast with every problem listed, and wire store, service, handlers, engine and http.Server with signal-driven shutdown.
lessons.title: Start from validated configuration and wire the whole service in one composition root
